Components
The future system is divided into nineteen domain contexts, each owning one area of the work, and a set of platform services they all use. Contexts talk to each other only through published contracts. A product fills a part of one context. It never joins several contexts together behind the scenes. This page describes the parts a product could fill, which context each serves, what any product would have to do to fill it, and who offers products for it.
This page describes the market. It does not assess, rank or recommend any product or supplier. Products are listed alphabetically, inclusion is not an endorsement, and leaving a product out is not a judgement. Any choice of product is made through the ministry’s procurement process.
How the parts fit
Where work happens Five case contexts, one per program family with workflow moving the work and correspondence sending notices and taking in documents
Money and challenges Payments & Benefit Issuance the one controlled path money leaves by Financial Components the benefit ledger Overpayment & Recovery money owed back Appeals & Reconsideration challenging a decision
What the work relies on Rules engine decides eligibility and entitlement Client identity resolution keeps one index of clients Consent & Disclosure keeps client consent in one place Evidence store holds every fact, in Evidence & Verification
What carries it all Event backbone carries events between contexts, checked against registered schemas
Facts enter as evidence and are held by Evidence & Verification. The decision service passes the rules engine a snapshot of them, and the engine turns it into a determination. The case contexts act on it, Financial Components and Payments & Benefit Issuance pay it, and correspondence tells the client. Events carry each step between contexts. No context reaches into another context’s data.
This is not the whole map. The Domains page shows all nineteen contexts, including those no product category here fills.
What every part must do
Whatever fills a part, these requirements apply.
Protected data is kept in Canada, and the most sensitive data is stored on-premise. NFR-C-004
A product sits inside one context, behind that context’s published contract, and exchanges only evidence and decisions with other contexts. NFR-I-002
If a product is a cloud service at the core of the solution, the ministry keeps an on-premise copy of its records: the context’s events, its decision records and its rules, kept current while the service runs. Mission-critical services, monthly payments first, can then carry on if the supplier cuts off access. NFR-A-009
Access rights are generated from information-sharing agreements, never granted by hand. FR-085NFR-SEC-003
Staff sign in through the provincial single sign-on service. NFR-SEC-001
The ministry’s records stay in formats it owns and can move, and open standards are preferred. NFR-I-005NFR-I-006
Every action is audit logged, and records are kept and destroyed on schedule. NFR-C-002NFR-C-003
Screens and documents meet accessibility standards. NFR-U-002

1
Case work, one context per program family
Five case contexts, each with its own case model
What it is for
The software caseworkers use every day. There are five case contexts, one for each program family: employment assistance, persons with disabilities, child care subsidy, employment services and child protection. Each keeps its own case record and its own lifecycle, from taking an application to scheduling reviews.
How it fits the whole
The five share ways of working, not a case model. Each records evidence through Evidence & Verification, asks Eligibility & Entitlement for decisions, raises work in Work Management and instructs payments through Financial Components. None of them holds payments, overpayments or reconsideration. Those are contexts of their own, described below. A case management product fills one case context. The same product can be used for more than one, but each use keeps its own data. Parameter N11 sets the rule for the rest: buy, adopt or reuse common tools, and build only where no ready-made product meets a legal, policy or programme need.
What any product must do
Takes applications in stages and keeps a complete case record, so work can carry on when a case changes hands. FR-025FR-032
Schedules reviews, recertifications and follow-up of missed appointments. FR-024
Five case contexts share protocols, not a case model. NFR-I-008
Does not make workers’ tasks slower than they are today. NFR-U-001

2
Payments & Benefit Issuance
The one controlled path money leaves by
What it is for
Issues every payment through one controlled path: issuance runs, direct deposit, cheque and electronic transfer, stop payment, reissue, returned items and the month-end cutoff. It reconciles with the corporate financial system.
How it fits the whole
It takes payment instructions from Financial Components and turns them into disbursements. It decides no entitlement. An entitlement decided twice must not be paid twice, and that guarantee lives here, once, rather than in five case contexts.
What any product must do
Issues every payment through one issuance service. FR-042
Runs issuance, with stop, recall, reissue and returns as separate operations. FR-043FR-044
Works with the corporate accounting system and the banks. INT-001INT-002
Who offers products
The project’s market research did not look at products for this part.
3
Financial Components
The benefit ledger
What it is for
Keeps the benefit ledger: accounts, accruals, payment schedules and double-entry postings. It creates, cancels and replaces payment instructions. It also holds money paid out now that may have to be repaid, such as interim assistance while a decision is being challenged.
How it fits the whole
It turns financial decisions into the postings that Payments & Benefit Issuance carries out. It is kept apart from issuance because a ledger and a payment run fail in different ways and are audited in different ways. It decides no entitlement.
What any product must do
Keeps a benefit ledger that reconciles three ways. FR-045
Holds money paid out now that may have to be repaid, until the awaited decision settles it. FR-041
Applies deductions and set-off, and protects the minimum a client must keep. FR-048
Separates working out, approving and releasing a payment, in code. FR-046
Who offers products
The project’s market research did not look at products for this part.
4
Overpayment & Recovery
Money owed back
What it is for
Raises overpayments, tells the client, and manages repayment agreements, deductions, set-off, write-off and referral to collections.
How it fits the whole
An overpayment always comes from recalculating a past period, and it always carries a classification. The rule that classifies it reads the evidence operation behind the recalculation. A supersession reported late gives a recoverable overpayment. A correction is classified by whose error it was. That rule is a versioned policy artefact, not code inside a case context.
What any product must do
Calculates and classifies overpayments from the evidence that changed. FR-051
A person decides every debt. FR-052
Handles repayment, write-off, collections and disputes. FR-053INT-019
Who offers products
The project’s market research did not look at products for this part.
5
Appeals & Reconsideration
Challenging a decision
What it is for
Records every reconsideration request, runs the legal time limits, builds the record for reconsideration and appeal, and deals with the tribunal as an outside party.
How it fits the whole
It is built once, not once per program. Whether reconsideration is available is decided by the independent reconsideration unit and recorded as evidence, which this context reads but never writes. A decision put right on appeal becomes a new decision, never a manual adjustment. Interim assistance is instructed from here and held in Financial Components.
What any product must do
Accepts and records every reconsideration request. FR-055
Reads, and never makes, the decision on whether reconsideration is available. FR-056
Builds the record for reconsideration and appeal from the decision record. FR-058
Treats the tribunal as an outside party, and puts decisions right without manual steps. FR-059FR-060
Who offers products
The project’s market research did not look at products for this part.
6
Consent & Disclosure
Consent, disclosure and requests for correction
What it is for
The one place client consent is kept: what was consented to, for how long, and when it was withdrawn. It records every disclosure, and a person’s request to correct their information, with its time limit.
How it fits the whole
Other contexts check consent here rather than keeping their own. The correction itself is made by the context that owns the fact. Agreements between organisations are a different thing: they sit in the agreement registry in Secure Data Exchange.
What any product must do
Records consents with their scope, time limit and withdrawal. FR-075
Discloses only with a recorded legal basis. FR-077
Handles requests for correction, and the annotations that follow. FR-079
Who offers products
The project’s market research did not look at products for this part.
7
Rules engine and decision authoring
Works out eligibility and entitlement
What it is for
Works out eligibility and entitlement from the facts, using the rules in force on the relevant dates. It also lets policy staff write, test and release those rules.
How it fits the whole
It sits inside Eligibility & Entitlement. The decision service around it gathers the facts first and passes the engine a snapshot of them. The engine reads nothing else while it runs, and returns determinations with their reasons. The case contexts and workflow ask for decisions, and hold no eligibility rules of their own. Architecture decision D3 covers whether to build or buy the authoring and release tooling.
What any product must do
Policy staff write rules as versioned artefacts with effective dates. FR-090
Runs inside the decision service, against a snapshot of the facts passed to it, and reads nothing else while it runs. FR-001
Each rule carries the policy it comes from and the date that policy took effect. FR-090
Works out effective dates by rule, for each part of a benefit. FR-005
Runs several generations of rules side by side. FR-010
Gives reasons that name the rule applied and the fact behind it. FR-002
Replays any past decision from stored records. FR-008
Blocks a release when rules have conflicting dates. FR-091
Keeps each rule in one authoritative place. NFR-M-005

8
Workflow and durable execution
Moves work between people and systems
What it is for
Moves work between people and systems: work items, queues, due dates set by legal time limits, and escalation. It also runs long processes, such as payment runs, that must survive failures and pick up where they stopped.
How it fits the whole
It serves Work Management, one context that all five case contexts use. It moves the work and asks for decisions, but makes no decisions itself. Its due dates come from the register of legal time limits.
What any product must do
Takes its due dates from one register of legal time limits. FR-061
Manages work items and queues, with due dates. FR-067
Supports supervision, escalation and overdue work. FR-068

Retries safely, and every dependency has a timeout and a fallback. NFR-I-004NFR-A-003

9
Event store, event backbone and schema registry
Holds the evidence, and carries events between contexts
What it is for
Evidence & Verification keeps every fact as an append-only stream of events, with its three dates. The backbone carries events between contexts, and the schema registry checks each one against its registered schema.
How it fits the whole
The backbone carries events. It is not where facts are kept. Facts are held by Evidence & Verification in its own event store, and other contexts read them through its published interface or keep copies built from its events. Four habits make this an architecture rather than a message bus. Every kind of event has a registered schema and one owning context. Each service saves its change and its event together, in one step. Work that crosses contexts is undone step by step if it fails, rather than locked across systems. And tampering shows, so the streams can serve as the audit trail. Architecture decision D9 sets the direction for the event broker and its support model.
What any product must do
Keeps each fact as a stream of versions, and works out its current state from them. DR-020
Records the four states of a fact, and corrections, without overwriting. FR-011FR-012
Fixes three dates on every fact before the first event. DR-001
Lets only evidence and determinations cross between contexts. NFR-I-002
Checks schema compatibility, and tests contracts. NFR-I-003
Shows if any record has been tampered with. NFR-SEC-009
Holds decades of data within stated limits on consumer lag. NFR-S-002NFR-P-005
Who offers products
Commercial products

Confluent Platform and Confluent Cloud Confluent Kafka distribution and managed Kafka service. Cloud service or self-hosted
KurrentDB Kurrent Event store database. Cloud service or self-hosted

10
Client identity resolution
Finds the records that belong to the same person
What it is for
Finds records that refer to the same person, so Participant Identity can join them. Uncertain matches go to a person to decide. Joining two records, or separating two that were wrongly joined, is recorded as an event that every other context follows.
How it fits the whole
It sits inside Participant Identity, which the ministry builds and keeps small: identifiers, enough detail to match on, and proof-of-identity status. Addresses, income and relationships are evidence, held elsewhere. Every other context refers to a client by the participant identifier. Proof of identity comes from the provincial identity services, not from this component. A matching library does the matching; it does not keep a master copy of each person.
What any product must do
Joins and separates client records, with people deciding uncertain matches, and records each join or separation as an event. FR-028
Supports establishing and proving identity. FR-027INT-005
Reads identity data when it is needed, rather than storing copies. DR-019

Correspondence, document capture and e-signature
Notices out, documents in, signatures
What it is for
Builds notices from the decision record, delivers them and records proof of service. It also captures documents from every channel and handles signatures and attestations.
How it fits the whole
It serves two contexts, Documents & Capture and Notices & Correspondence. Notices take their content from determinations and the rules that produced them, so a notice always matches its decision. A captured document supports evidence. It is never a decision.

Current State
This page describes how the work is done today. It is context, not the source of the design. The design comes from the law, from policy and from the nature of the work. What is here serves as a check on it. A large, expensive piece of software, laboured over by hundreds of capable and well-meaning people, can still fail the organizations it serves, and the reason usually lies in what it leaves out: what it ignores, and what it pushes outside itself. A replacement must not do the same.
What the SDPR procedures are
Every recurring task a caseworker does has a written procedure: what starts it, which screens to open, which form to send, what to type in which field. Together they run to 8.2 million characters. They describe the service as staff really deliver it.
Each one carries a header naming its purpose, the policy it carries out, the law behind it, and how the system classifies the work. That turns the whole set into a map of the services.
326procedures
15capability areas
128kinds of work request
84statutory provisions cited
146distinct forms
13ways to reach the ministry
Work crosses system boundaries constantly
63% of documented procedures need two or more systems to finish one task.
Number of procedures by count of separate systems required, across 326 procedures.

Highlighted rows are the 207 procedures that cross a system boundary. Four procedures require seven.
Counted by naming every system referenced in each procedure. The most common pairing is the Siebel case system with the client portal, then the case system with Service Canada, then the case system with the mainframe.
One journey, three systems, two re-keys
Recovering an overpayment is the clearest example. A worker who has decided someone was paid too much has to:
Open a separate web application to calculate the amount. It does not connect to either system of record.
Print the result, scan it, and attach it back to the case.
Move the case file to their own office in the mainframe so they have permission to act on it.
Type the amount into the mainframe by hand.
Move the case file back to where it came from.
Clients whose earnings are annualised need one step more: a spreadsheet. The worker reads figures off one screen, types them into the sheet, and types the result back.
None of this is anyone's poor practice. The procedure says to do it this way, because with the systems that exist this is the right way.
Where the rules actually live
A modernisation has to know what it is replacing. The rules that decide entitlement sit in six separate places. Only one of them is a rules engine, and the one that carries authority, the policy manual, can only be read by a person.
Business rules by location
Where
What it holds
A rules engine
29 separate rulebases covering eligibility, validation, debt and payment calculation
The mainframe
Benefit calculation, rate recalculation, time limits, sanction end dates
Formulas inside the case system
Retention periods, access levels, privacy calculations
A database table
The rates the public-facing eligibility estimator uses
Spreadsheets on SharePoint
Eighteen workbooks with no version control or audit trail. Five of them decide entitlement
The policy manual
The authoritative rules, dated in prose, with only a partial archive
Found by reading the technical design documents for the current release alongside the procedures and the policy manual. Nothing on record gives the 29 rulebases source control, a promotion pipeline or a version register.
Routing runs on a spreadsheet
An Excel workbook decides which queue a request joins, how urgent it is, how long it has, and where a scanned document goes. Fifty-six procedures point at it. One of its sheets maps 445 form numbers to their handling. So the priorities and service-level targets for the whole service sit outside the platform, kept up by hand.
Accommodation and the signature problem
There is a path for applicants who need an interpreter, find reading difficult, or have little access to a computer. A worker reads the questions aloud and enters the answers for them.
That path skips portal registration, so the applicant never gets a personal identification number. The electronic signature depends on that number. So the people the accommodation exists for are the people who then cannot sign electronically.
How these figures were produced
The counts come from reading the Resource Finder and the other document stores in full, then pattern-matching and mapping the text. Named systems, capability areas and the policy behind each procedure come from the documents and the policy manual.
Nobody has measured the volumes yet. You can count caseload throughput, worker streams, transaction rates and queue depth directly. The figures here come from the technical design documents instead.
The rest of the site sets out the design. It is worked out from the law, policy and the nature of the work, and the conditions on this page check it rather than shape it. Start with evidence. The overpayment journey above is what happens when a record cannot say what the ministry knew, or when.

Determinations
Someone can challenge a decision about their entitlement years after the ministry made it. So the design treats every decision as something you re-run, not something you remember.
The problem with asking a system what it decided
Ask a typical case management system why a person got a particular amount in March 2022 and it will work the sum again. It uses today's rules, today's data and today's software, then reports the answer with confidence. The answer may well be right. Nobody can tell, and nobody can show a tribunal the difference.
Three things have shifted underneath since March 2022. Policy changed. The person's recorded circumstances changed, perhaps several times. And someone upgraded the software. A rules engine upgrade can change how the same rule reads, and nobody notices until a client appeals.
Treating a decision as a function
The design makes entitlement a calculation with no hidden inputs. It reads the rules, the facts and the date it is deciding for. While it runs it does not read the clock, query a database, or call another service. It gets everything it needs up front.
That rule sounds academic. It is what makes the next part work: if nothing hidden went in, then storing what went in is enough to reproduce what came out.
The function signature
Determine(rulesArtefactVersion, evidenceSnapshot, referenceDate) → DeterminationResult
Pure: no input or output, no clock reads, no database access, no service calls. No rules engine gives you this on its own. The shell around the engine enforces it. The engine runs in-process against a snapshot passed by value, and that is what puts byte-identical replay within reach rather than in the brochure.
Five things stored with every decision
Storing the answer is not enough. Storing the answer and the rules is still not enough. The system binds five artefacts into the record at the moment it makes the decision.
1 The rules Content digest, tagged and immutable once released Stored
2 The engine Version number and the archived binary Stored
3 The facts it saw Copied in full into the record, never referenced Stored
4 The reasoning Which rules fired and which branches were taken, in a ministry-owned format Stored
5 The letter Content-hashed template, resolved at decision time Stored
The decision can be replayed.
Four years on, the same inputs produce the same answer, the reasoning can be read aloud, and the letter the client received can be reproduced.
Switch any artefact off to see which question stops being answerable. Each one covers a failure the other four do not.
Teams leave out the fifth one most often. A decision that reproduces perfectly, next to a letter nobody can rebuild, still misses the question the tribunal asked. That question is often about what the person was told, not about what the system worked out.
How long replay has to work
Archiving the software tells you what it was. It does not promise that anything in twenty years can still run it. The operating system, the processor and the container runtime all die younger than a child protection record, which the ministry keeps for ninety years.
Rather than leave that hanging, the design commits to a horizon in three stages and writes it down in advance.
Years 0–7
We archive the software itself and test it every quarter to confirm it still runs. Seven years covers the appeal, reconsideration and audit paths that really do re-run a decision.
Years 7–20
The rules live on as a written specification, with a test suite that any rebuild has to pass. The suite stays independent of the engine from day one, so this handover costs nothing when it comes.
Beyond 20 years
The stored reasoning, the letter and the facts are the record. Re-running stops being on offer. This is what a paper file has always been.
The three stages run in order, which is why they are numbered. The last one holds up because the ministry declared it in advance, rather than discovering it during a hearing.
Re-running a decision proves what the rules worked out. It does not prove the rules matched the policy in force at the time. So every rule carries the policy it comes from and the date that policy took effect. The ministry does not publish old versions of its policy manual, and its archive of old rate tables has gaps. So for each family of rules the horizon also records how far back the policy itself can still be produced. Before that date, the stored reasoning, the letter and the facts are the record, and the ministry says so in advance.
Where the policy version is kept
The policy citation and its effective-date marker sit inside the rules artefact, which the decision record binds by its content digest. There is no sixth artefact. The horizon statement records, per rule family, the earliest effective date for which the governing policy text or rate can be produced from a retained source. Historical rates are harvested once, at ingest, rather than fetched later from an archive with no retention commitment.
Two decisions made moments apart can disagree
Storing the inputs makes replay reliable. It says nothing about whether the inputs were gathered consistently. That is where the remaining gap sits.
Gathering the facts means reading across several stores that update on their own schedules. Two decisions issued seconds apart, with one store briefly behind, can each see a different world quite legitimately. Both replay perfectly. Both are reproducible. They disagree, and nothing described so far catches it. So the design pins each snapshot to a point in the sequence of recorded events. A later reader can then tell which view of the world a decision was made against.
Before a decision: a letter that is not one
Sometimes the ministry writes to a client before it decides: this is what we found, this is what it may mean, reply by this date. That letter is not a decision, and the system keeps it separate from one. It carries its reasons, its reply-by date and a plain statement that no decision has been made. Whatever the client sends back is recorded as evidence for the decision that follows.
A client can still ask for a reconsideration at that point. The request is always recorded, and nobody turns it away at the counter. Whether a reconsideration is available is decided by the independent reconsideration unit, not by the worker who sent the letter.
When a decision is challenged
A decision that is overturned is never edited. The original stays in the record as what was decided, with everything it was based on. The new decision sits beside it, with its own record, and says what caused it. The client's history shows both, in order, with reasons. The money owed either way is worked out from the difference between the two.
The appeal tribunal can confirm the ministry's decision or rescind it. It cannot change it part way, and it cannot send it back. An appeal can also end without the tribunal deciding, because the client withdrew it or abandoned it. The system records how the appeal ended and, only if the tribunal decided, what it decided. A rescinded decision is marked, never erased, and the ministry then decides again.
A client waiting for a reconsideration or an appeal may keep receiving assistance at the old level. That money is paid on a promise to repay whatever the final decision does not support. The system holds it as repayable from the day it is paid, linked to the decision it is waiting for, and settles it automatically when that decision is made.
How challenges are modelled
PreDecisionCommunication belongs to Eligibility & Entitlement, in the shell around Determine, never inside it. Its amount is a class (iii) output, it carries a no_decision_made marker, and its reply window is a statutory clock artefact. Reconsideration availability is a DiscretionaryDetermination recorded in Evidence & Verification by the Reconsideration and Administrative Fairness Unit; Appeals & Reconsideration reads it and never writes it. Appeal outcome is two attributes: disposition (decided, withdrawn, abandoned) and panel determination (confirmed, rescinded). Interim assistance is a RepayableIssuance in Financial Components, resolved on the awaited DeterminationIssued; on denial it becomes an overpayment component classified by policy.
Decisions that affect people carry their own classification
Every rule carries a label saying what kind of decision it produces. Some produce an administrative decision, which needs reasons. Some produce a decision a person has to make before it takes effect. The rest are working sums that affect nobody on their own.
That label travels with the decision into the letter. A decision that goes against someone sends out its reasons, its appeal period and the route to challenge it, because the label says it must. Not because somebody remembered.

Domains
Perhaps the biggest choice in this design is where to draw the lines between parts of the system. Fifteen families of domain model. One family is really five case models, one per program, which makes nineteen models in all.
The problem of a single model
Programmes like this usually start by building one model of a case that every program can share. That is how MIS began, and how ICM began. It looks like the responsible choice: less duplication, one place to change things, one way of working across the ministry.
What happens next is well documented. A child protection investigation and a child care subsidy renewal have almost nothing in common beyond involving a person. Make them share a lifecycle and every change to one has to be negotiated with everyone else. Multiply that over dozens of programs and nobody can change the model at all. So teams bolt on sub-entities, extend them, and add more ways to integrate. The system turns into a plate of spaghetti. You cannot change anything in one place, and any failure reaches everywhere. This is not hypothetical. ICM merged its final two phases and cut child protection scope for exactly this reason.
This design takes the difference seriously. Five program families get five case models. The plumbing is written more than once, and that is cheaper than the alternative.
What the parts are
Identity, evidence and decisions
Participant Identity
Evidence & Verification
Eligibility & Entitlement
One per program family
Employment assistance
Child protection
Child care subsidy
Employment services
Persons with disabilities
Money
Payments & Benefit Issuance
Financial Components
Overpayment & Recovery
Delivery
Appeals & Reconsideration
Work Management
Documents & Capture
Notices & Correspondence
Provider & Outcome Management
Information governance
Consent & Disclosure
Investigation & Loss Management
Channel Entitlement & Service Restriction
Evidence & Verification
Every dated claim about the world, and how it was checked.
Owns
The evidence succession set, the registered evidence types (including a worker’s recorded judgement), verification policy, the operations, three time axes.
Does not own
It does not decide anything. It records what was claimed and what was verified.
Boundary test
Its events are the trigger fabric for everything else.
Select any part to see what it owns, what it deliberately does not own, and the test that tells you when the boundary has been breached. The five case models share protocols, not a case model.
Twelve families were drawn when the architecture was first issued, which made sixteen models. Three more were added later, because nothing in the map modelled how the ministry holds what it knows: Consent & Disclosure, Investigation & Loss Management, and Channel Entitlement & Service Restriction. The family name “Case & Service Delivery” never owns anything. The owner is always one of the five case models.
Six rules keep the lines in place
A boundary that lives only in a diagram will not survive delivery pressure. These six are written so a reviewer can point at something and say whether it complies.
Each part can be released on its own
It has its own storage and its own message topics. If two parts always ship together, they are one part wearing two names.
No part reads another part's database
No shared tables. No joins across schemas. Not for a report, and not in a test environment. This rule erodes first, and takes the longest to notice.
There are exactly two ways to talk
A published interface for reads, and published events for notices. There is no third way, and adding one is not a shortcut.
Copies are owned by whoever holds them
A part that needs another's data keeps its own copy, built from that part's events and shaped the way it needs. When the source corrects something, the copy has to follow.
Reference data has one master
Rate tables, program codes, value lists and reason codes are each kept in one place and published as events. Nobody maintains a second copy by hand. They change when policy changes, not when the software does.
Every copy is stamped
When a part copies evidence, it records where the copy came from: which part, which piece of evidence, which version, when the source learned it, and when the copy was taken. That is what makes rule four checkable. A correction can find every copy by looking it up, not by asking every team.
The thin identity model
Participant Identity stays deliberately small. It holds identifiers, enough detail to tell two people apart, and whether anyone has proven the identity. No addresses, no income, no relationships.
This part is the most likely to drift, because every new requirement brings a reason to add one more field to the person record. Once that starts, the shared model is back, in the one place the design most needs to stay thin.
Merge and split go in on day one rather than later. The audit of the previous system found duplicate records at scale, and called its search ineffective and exact-match only. Adding merge afterwards to a system that assumed one person equals one row is close to impossible. By then every payment instruction and every stored decision has keyed itself to an identifier the design promised would hold still.
Published events and the boundary test
Participant Identity publishes PersonRegistered, IdentityMerged, IdentitySplit, IdentifierAdded and IdentifierInvalidated. Every other context keeps its own projection (Payee, Applicant, Caregiver, Reporter, Appellant, Debtor), keyed by participant identifier.
Evidence & Verification publishes EvidenceRecorded, EvidenceActivated, EvidenceSuperseded, EvidenceVerified, EvidenceInvalidated and EvidenceCorrectionRecorded.
Parts that are not domain models
Some pieces are shared infrastructure rather than parts of the business. Platform teams own them and everyone uses them. The difference matters. A platform part that starts holding program state has quietly become a twentieth domain model, and nobody chartered it.
The platform parts are the published interface (the Open Host Service), the translation layer over the old system (the Legacy Anti-Corruption Layer), Secure Data Exchange for sharing with other organisations, Rules Authoring & Release, the Component Library, the Analytical Platform, and Correlation & Migration State, which keeps track of which old record matches which new one. Three more services hold no program state of their own: severing, routing a correction to the parts that own the fact, and carrying out retention and disposal.
Two of them are worth naming, because their charters point in opposite directions on purpose. The published interface is permanent: it is the contract built to outlive whatever implements it. The translation layer over the existing Siebel system is temporary, and the team that builds it answers for winding itself up.
A team accountable for a thing will grow and protect it. A team measured on its own dissolution will not.

title: Evidence — The Future of Case Management IT

Evidence
ICM tracks facts. It overwrites fields and buries history. In the new system the unit of information is a dated claim, tied to its evidence and to whoever made it. Later work can disprove that claim, confirm it, overturn it or replace it, and nothing is lost on the way.
Why not store facts?
A system that stores only the current state, "Income: $900", leaves the important questions open. How do we know? What evidence is there? When did we know? Is this the corrected number, or the number we recorded at the time?
Front-line staff adapt, so the information is not lost. It is just not modelled. It goes into notes, forms and attachments, and only a thin slice of it is ever held as data.
This is not an auditing nicety. It closes the gap between how the system holds data and how front-line staff work. Substantiating evidence against claims is the most common task a worker performs, and the system does not model it at all, so it is done by hand. Social workers spend hours mapping their notes onto a structure that serves the software rather than their clients.
So the unit the system records, and the unit its parts exchange, is an assertion:
what household composition: couple
about whomparticipant 4471-A
true forfrom 1 January, open-ended
learned on12 September
fromeligibility review finding
verifiedtenancy agreement, 14 September
One evidence assertion, from a case where the dates are in dispute. The ministry now says the household was a couple from January. It reached that view in September. In between it paid eight months at the single rate. Which of those two dates you read decides what happens next.
The four things that can happen to an assertion
Once the system records something, nobody edits it in place. Four operations change what the system believes. They differ in one respect: what each does to the period the claim covers.
[aria-label] Evidence operations
Record
Supersede
Correct
Invalidate
The world changed.
valid time
a new period
transaction time
now
The earlier assertion stays true for its own period. The new one takes over from a later date.
For example A partner moves in on 1 May, and the client reports it.
If this produced an overpayment, the classification rule reads the operation as the world having changed.
Select an operation. Supersede and Correct both replace an earlier claim, but only Correct says the earlier claim was wrong about its own period. That is what separates a recoverable debt from the ministry's own error.
That distinction is why the model exists. It is a policy rule written into the shape of the data. It applies consistently because the record itself names the operation that caused the recalculation. Nobody has to guess at it afterwards.
The operation feeds the classification without settling it. Who caused the error matters too. A client who hid a relationship is not in the same position as a worker who mis-keyed a figure. The model promises something narrower and more useful: the question has an answer at all, and the answer comes from the record rather than from whoever opens the file today.
Where a conventional record gives up
Take the assertion above to a tribunal. The client accepts a relationship exists but disputes that it began in January. Three separate things are now in question, and they are easy to confuse:
What the ministry believed about the household in each of those eight months.
When the ministry changed its mind, and on what evidence.
What start date the ministry now asserts.
A conventional design holds one relationship start date, plus an audit entry saying a worker changed it on 12 September. That answers the third question, gestures at the second, and cannot touch the first. It leaves the eight monthly payments looking like errors. Each one was the right answer to what the ministry knew at the time.
The operations, formally
Operation
Valid time
Transaction time
Meaning
RecordEvidence
asserted period
now
We learned a new fact
SupersedeEvidence
new period
now
The world changed
CorrectEvidence
same period
now
We were wrong about the world
InvalidateEvidence
closed
now
The assertion should never have existed
The aggregate is the evidence succession set: the stream of versions of one logical fact about one subject. Commands append events; current state is a projection. Verification status transitions are themselves events.
The third date, and the history problem
Two time axes are standard. This design carries a third, because the new system inherits fifteen years of records from systems that are still running.
Old records all arrive on the same day. Make that migration date the "when we learned it" date and every historical fact looks as though it arrived at the same moment. Supersede and Correct then look identical across the whole pre-cutover record. The overpayment rule stops working on exactly the records where most overpayments sit.
The third axis holds the date the old system asserted the fact, where the old record still shows it. Often it cannot be read at all, so the date carries a confidence marker. Where the answer is unknown, the system says so rather than guessing.
valid time
The period in the world for which the fact holds.
Set by whoever asserts it, from the source.
transaction time
When this system learned it.
Set at recording. Never changes.
legacy assertion time
When the previous system asserted it, if that can be decoded.
Set at migration. Often unknown, and marked as such.
Three dates on every assertion. The third can be empty, and the design treats an unknown value as unknown rather than swapping in the migration date.
Nobody can add this later. Events are immutable: you can introduce a field with a default, but you cannot fill it in afterwards. Either the migration decoded the source or it did not. So the decision has to come before the first production record.
Confidence values and replay behaviour
legacy_asserted_at travels with legacy_assertion_confidence, which takes DECODED (read straight from the legacy record or audit trail), INFERRED (worked out from a related artefact by a written rule) or UNKNOWN.
On UNKNOWN, any consumer working out a knowledge-state answer must return INDETERMINATE. That covers the overpayment rule, a tribunal reconstruction view and a disclosure history. An overpayment whose classification is INDETERMINATE is treated as administrative error unless a person reclassifies it on recorded evidence. Valid-time questions, such as recalculating an amount, go ahead and are marked TEMPORALLY_UNVERIFIED. For a migrated fact, recorded_at is always the import time.
Backdated recalculation runs off valid time, which any competent migration preserves, so recalculation survives. Something narrower breaks without the third axis: what the ministry knew and when. That is the question separating a recoverable debt from the ministry's own error.
Every kind of evidence is registered, including judgement
Each kind of evidence, such as income or household composition, is registered before anyone can use it. The registration sets its shape, what counts as verifying it, how sensitive it is, how long it is kept and how it ends, and whose record it is. None of that is guessed later from where the data happens to sit.
One registered kind matters more than it looks: a worker’s judgement. Much of the work is a worker using a discretion the law gives them. The system records that as evidence too, as a discretionary determination. It names the law that gives the discretion, the authority the worker acted under, who decided, the evidence they weighed, and their reasons in their own words. A decision that rests on judgement can then be re-run like one that rests on arithmetic. Without it, the judgement ends up in case notes, and the decision rests on something nobody can find.
When a fact is corrected, every copy has to act
Other parts of the system keep their own copies of evidence (see Domains). When the source corrects a fact, every part holding a copy must be told, and must act. This is enforced. A part that holds a copy without listening for corrections fails its own release checks.
What happens to decisions already made from the old copy is a policy choice. Each program family sets it, and keeps it as a versioned rule. There are three answers. Re-open: make a fresh decision on the corrected facts. Annotate only: the outcome does not change, so the decision record notes the correction and why nothing followed. Flag for review: nobody can tell mechanically whether it matters, often because a worker’s judgement was one of the inputs, so a person decides.
Registered types, discretion and correction, formally
Evidence types live in a schema registry with versioned definitions. Each carries its schema, verification policy, security classification, retention and disposition class, custodianship and provenance requirements.
DiscretionaryDetermination is a registered type with a mandatory schema: discretion_head, authority_relied_on, decision_maker, rationale, factors_considered and outcome, with supervisory_endorsement where the discretion class requires it. It is carried by value in the input snapshot like any other evidence. Whether reconsideration is available is one such determination, recorded by the Reconsideration and Administrative Fairness Unit.
EvidenceCorrectionRecorded is a mandatory subscription for every context that holds a copy, checked at release by a fitness function. Every copy carries five stamps: source_context, source_evidence_id, source_evidence_version, source_transaction_time and copied_at. Each program family publishes its mapping from evidence type to Re-open, Annotate-only or Flag-for-review as a versioned policy artefact, and the mapping in force is recorded on the correction annotation.

Glossary
The parameters and requirements use some words that have a particular meaning in this work. This page explains each one in plain terms. Where architects have their own name for an idea, it is given in brackets, so you can recognise it in other documents.

Accessibility standard
The rules a screen or form must follow so that people with disabilities can use it.
The Province sets a standard for how accessible its online services must be. It is based on the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG), an international set of rules. They cover things like text a screen reader can read aloud, colours with enough contrast, and forms you can fill in with a keyboard alone.
N15 asks for this from the first release, not as a fix added later.
Used in:
[aria-label] N15: Everyone can use the service, whatever their ability or way in
N15 In requirements: BR-009 · NFR-U-002
Active-active
Running a service at two or more sites at once, so either can carry the load if the other fails.
In requirements: NFR-A-004
Adjudicability
Four facts recorded for each entitlement: whether it is granted under a statute, whether its decisions can be reconsidered, whether they can be appealed, and to whom.
In requirements: FR-006 · FR-030 · FR-033 · FR-056 · FR-063 · FR-092
Adjudicating authority
A body allowed to decide or review a class of decisions. It can be inside the ministry or outside it, such as Pacific Blue Cross or CLBC.
In requirements: FR-056
Administrative review
A review, under the regulation to the CFCSA, of a director's decision, act or failure to act, conducted by a review authority the director designates. A person who was involved in the matter cannot be designated, and the review authority recommends but does not decide the matter.
Adverse decision
A decision that denies, reduces or ends assistance, or creates a debt.
Aggregate
A cluster of data the system treats as one unit for changes, with its own rules that must always hold. Each aggregate has exactly one writer at any moment, per cohort (N05). Examples: an evidence succession set, a payment instruction, a disbursement, a repayable issuance.
In requirements: BR-011 · FR-006 · FR-041 · NFR-SEC-011 · DR-020
API, REST, GraphQL
An API is how systems ask each other for data or actions; REST and GraphQL are two common styles.
In requirements: NFR-SEC-002 · NFR-I-003 · INT-003
Appeal
Asking an independent body outside the ministry to look at a decision again.
If a client still disagrees after a reconsideration, they can often appeal. An appeal goes to a body outside the ministry, usually a tribunal. Not every decision can be appealed, and not every appeal goes to the same body. That is why N20 records this for each entitlement.
Used in:
[aria-label] N17: Different people decide, review and pay
N17 ·
[aria-label] N20: Each benefit records whether and how a decision can be challenged
N20
Appeal record
Everything the ministry had in front of it when it made a decision, gathered for the client.
When a client challenges a decision, policy says the ministry must give them the appeal record. It holds all the submissions, information and records the ministry had when it made the decision. Before the client gets it, some protected details may have to be removed. That step is called severing.
N08 asks that the system can put this record together on demand, rather than staff searching for the pieces by hand.
Used in:
[aria-label] N08: The decision record is complete on its own
N08
Asserted negative
A question asked and answered "no". It counts as evidence, unlike a blank that was never asked.
In requirements: FR-011 · DR-002
Assisted digital
A worker or representative completing an online transaction for someone, with the helper's identity recorded.
Assistive technology
Tools people with disabilities use to work a computer or phone, such as screen readers.
Examples are screen readers that read the page aloud, software that magnifies the screen, voice control, and switches used instead of a mouse. Automated scans find only about 30% of accessibility problems. The rest show up only when a person tries the service with these tools, which is why N15 asks for real testing.
Used in:
[aria-label] N15: Everyone can use the service, whatever their ability or way in
N15 In requirements: BR-009 · NFR-U-002
At Home Program
A program for children and youth with support needs. Eligibility is decided on a qualified assessor's assessment and a Regional Eligibility Committee's recommendation, or by Direct Admit, and an eligible decision opens the child's Medical Benefits (FR-283 to FR-285).
Automated check
A test that software runs by itself to catch a rule being broken.
Technical teams use several kinds. A lint rule reads the code and flags patterns that break a rule, such as one part reaching into another part’s tables. A fitness function is a test of the whole design, run again and again, that fails if the design drifts away from a goal. A compatibility check compares a new version of an interface with the old one and fails if the change would break anyone who uses it.
N18 says that wherever a rule can be checked this way, it must be. A person then only has to check what a machine cannot.
Used in:
[aria-label] N18: Every rule comes with a way to catch it being broken
N18 In requirements: NFR-A-003 · NFR-M-004 · DR-007
Availability target
How much of the time a service must be up and working.
It is usually given as a percentage over a month or a year. A service that must be available 99.9% of the time can be down for about 45 minutes a month. N16 asks that each service’s target be set by how much harm an outage does to a client, not picked the same for everything.
Used in:
[aria-label] N16: Each service has recovery targets, proven in practice runs
N16 In requirements: NFR-A-007 · INT-005
Back end for front end
A small server behind each user interface that holds the sign-in tokens, so they never sit in the browser.
In requirements: NFR-SEC-001 · INT-005
BCEA Policy and Procedure Manual
The ministry's published policy manual for employment and disability assistance. Under the source hierarchy it overrides procedures and job aids, and legislation overrides it.
In requirements: BR-007 · BR-013 · BR-014
BCeID, BC Services Card, IDIR
Provincial sign-in credentials: BCeID for individuals and businesses, the BC Services Card for citizens with verified identity, and IDIR for government staff.
In requirements: NFR-SEC-001 · INT-005
Benefit component
One part of an assistance payment, such as support, shelter or a supplement. Each component can take effect on a different date.
In requirements: FR-005
Break-glass access
Emergency access to a restricted record outside normal rules, always logged and reviewed afterwards.
In requirements: NFR-SEC-004
Business rule
A rule about how the ministry’s work is done, such as who qualifies for a benefit.
Business rules come from law, policy and practice. “A client must report income by the fifth of the month” is one. N04 asks that each rule lives in one place, with the data it controls, so there is never a question about which copy of the rule is the real one.
Used in:
[aria-label] N04: Rules live with the data they control
N04
Byte-identical
Exactly the same, down to every character, with nothing that differs.
Calendar basis
Which calendar a time limit counts in, such as business days, calendar months or the school year.
In requirements: FR-024 · FR-039 · FR-061
Capture, states S0–S3
Moving a part of the service to the new system for a cohort, through four states: old system in charge (S0), shadow (S1), captured with write-back (S2), new system in charge (S3).
In requirements: DR-014
Care provider
An extended family member or other person who has a relationship with, or a cultural or traditional responsibility to, a child, is not already the child's guardian, and agrees to care for the child in an out-of-care arrangement. A care provider is not a caregiver.
Caregiver
A person with whom a child is placed by a director and who, by agreement with the director, is authorized to carry out the rights and responsibilities, under the agreement, of the director (CFCSA section 1). Often called a foster caregiver.
Case context
One of the five program-family domain contexts (employment assistance, persons with disabilities, child care subsidy, employment services, child protection) that together form the Case & Service Delivery family. They share protocols, not a case model; the family name is never an owner (NFR-I-008; ADR-001).
CFCSA
The Child, Family and Community Service Act, BC's child protection law. Section 96 lets child protection workers request information.
In requirements: NFR-SEC-013 · INT-013 · INT-027 · INT-031 · INT-038 · DR-023
Channel
A way a person reaches the ministry: online, by phone, in person or by mail.
N15 asks that a person can finish the same task through every supported channel and get the same result. It also asks that every service has a supported way in that is not online.
Used in:
[aria-label] N15: Everyone can use the service, whatever their ability or way in
N15
Child in care
A child who is in the custody, care or guardianship of a director or a director of adoption (CFCSA section 1).
Child in the Home of a Relative (CIHR)
A closed program supporting children living with relatives. It runs on rules frozen in 2010 alongside the current rules.
In requirements: FR-010 · FR-023 · INT-013
CI (continuous integration)
The automated pipeline that builds and tests every change before it can be released.
In requirements: NFR-SEC-002 · NFR-U-002 · NFR-M-004 · NFR-I-002
Circuit breaker, bulkhead, timeout
Protections that stop one failing service from taking others down with it.
In requirements: NFR-P-001 · NFR-A-003
Client index
A single index for finding people and spotting duplicate records, with uncertain matches sent to a person to decide.
In requirements: FR-028 · INT-016 · DR-019
Cohort review
Holding a large group of new debts that share one cause for review before any notices go out.
Common tools
Tools almost every organisation needs, like sign-in and document storage, that can be bought rather than built.
N11 lists them: workflow (moving work between people), notifications, identity and sign-in, storing passwords and encryption keys safely, policy checks (software that decides whether an action is allowed), scheduling, document storage, search, and print and mail.
Good products for all of these already exist. Building one in-house is allowed only for a need no product meets, and someone outside the team has to agree.
Used in:
[aria-label] N11: Buy common tools, and have someone else check any choice to build
N11
Community agreement
Policy's name for an agreement a director makes under section 92.1 of the CFCSA with a First Nation, the Nisga'a Nation, a Treaty First Nation or a legal entity representing another Indigenous community. It provides for consultation and cooperation on named kinds of work or for the community to provide services, and it applies to all directors except in its services part.
Component library (tiered)
Shared, reusable interface building blocks, split into tiers so accessibility logic sits in the shared lower tiers.
In requirements: NFR-U-005
Conditional requirement
A requirement in groups CF15 to CF18 that applies only if a scope decision brings its area into the replacement: child and youth mental health (DEP-26), the Integrated Child and Youth teams (DEP-27) or youth justice (DEP-28).
Considered but not retainable
Evidence that policy lets staff look at but not keep, such as tax information that must not be printed.
In requirements: DR-002
Continuing custody order
A court order under the CFCSA under which the director becomes the child's sole personal guardian and the Public Guardian and Trustee becomes the child's sole property guardian.
Control totals
Counts and sums struck before a run is approved and checked unchanged afterwards.
In requirements: BR-007 · FR-043 · FR-103 · NFR-C-003 · NFR-M-003 · DR-004
Coordination agreement
An agreement contemplated by the federal Act among Canada, the Province and an Indigenous governing body, to coordinate the exercise of Indigenous jurisdiction over child and family services. A community does not need one to make laws, and the agreement must carry conditions on the use, disclosure and security of information.
Copy
A fact one part of the system holds that it took from another part.
Parts of the system often keep their own copy of a fact so they can work quickly without asking the source every time. That is normal. The risk is that the source corrects the fact and the copy stays wrong. N06 asks that every copy records where it came from, so a correction can always find it.

[aria-label] N06: Every copy can be traced, and every correction reaches it

N21 In requirements: NFR-C-004
Corporate Accounting System (CAS)
The Province's financial system of record. All payments are posted and reconciled against it.
In requirements: BR-004 · FR-042 · NFR-A-005 · NFR-S-003 · NFR-C-008 · INT-001
Correction
Fixing a fact that was recorded wrongly, as opposed to a fact that changed.
These two are easy to confuse, and they mean different things. A correction says the record was wrong all along: the income was never $900, it was $1,100. A supersession says the world changed: the income was $900 until March and $1,100 after.
Both can leave a client underpaid or overpaid in the past. The difference is who bears it. A supersession the client reported late gives an overpayment the ministry can recover. A correction is judged by whose error it was: a client who hid something is in a different position from a worker who mis-keyed a figure. The old system cannot tell the two apart, which is why N14 says that difference is lost if a group moves back.

Data load (migration)
Moving existing records from the old system into the new one.
Migration scripts copy large amounts of data in bulk. If a rule is enforced only by the screens staff use, a bulk load can skip right past it. N04 asks that the data enforce its own rules, so every route in is checked.
Used in:

N04
Data model
A part’s own description of the things it works with, such as a person or a payment.
Different parts of the ministry’s work need to know different things about the same person. Payments needs a bank account. A case worker needs contact details. A single shared model tries to hold all of it, and every change then needs everyone to agree.
N03 asks each part to keep its own model instead. The Domains page shows the nineteen parts and what each one owns.

N03
Data-sharing agreement
A formal agreement setting out what information one organisation may share with another, and why.
Today these agreements are usually signed documents. Staff read them and then set up access by hand. N13 asks that each agreement is also written in a form the system can read, and that the system grants access from the agreement itself. That way every access can be traced to an agreement and checked.

Database layout (schema)
The structure of a database: its tables, its columns, and what each one holds.
Technical teams call this a schema. When one part sends another a copy of its database rows, or relies on its layout, the two become tied together. Neither can change its layout without breaking the other. N02, N03 and N10 all guard against this.

N07 In requirements: FR-001 · FR-011 · FR-025 · FR-042 · FR-051 · FR-057 · FR-062 · FR-073and 11 more
Decision class (A, B, C)
How a rule output is treated: A is an administrative decision needing reasons, B needs a human decision-maker before it is issued, C is an intermediate calculation never shown as a decision.
In requirements: FR-003
Decision record
The stored account of a decision: what was decided, on what facts, under which rules.
Every decision the system makes is saved with everything needed to explain it later. That includes the version of the rules and of the engine that ran them, a full copy of the facts it used, its reasoning, and the version of the letter template the client was sent. It also records how far through the record of events the decision read (the watermark) and what kind of decision it was, so that a decision needing reasons, or a person’s sign-off, can be told apart from a working sum.
N08 asks that the record holds full copies of all of this, not links to other systems. That way it still makes sense years later, after those systems have changed or gone.

The B.C. law that commits the Province to bring its laws in line with the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples.
Passed in 2019, often shortened to DRIPA or the Declaration Act. In requirements: INT-028
Destroying records (disposition)
What happens to a record at the end of its life: destroyed, archived or handed over.
Records cannot be kept forever. The law sets how long each kind must be kept and what happens after. Architects call this disposition. A record may be destroyed, moved to the archives, or handed to another government that is its rightful custodian.
N12 asks that the way each kind of record ends is decided before the system stores anything, because the method shapes how the records are stored.

N13 In requirements: FR-072 · FR-096 · NFR-C-003
Destroying the key (crypto-shredding)
Locking one person’s records with their own key, then destroying the key to make the records unreadable.
Each person’s records are scrambled (encrypted) with a key that belongs to them alone. When the records must be destroyed, the system destroys the key. The scrambled data can stay in place, but nobody can read it ever again. This lets a permanent history meet a legal duty to destroy.
N12 allows it for a small number of kinds of fact, each named, where a duty to destroy one person’s records can be foreseen. It is never the default. It needs careful planning about who holds the keys and how destruction is proven.
Used in:

A programme such as income assistance contains many separate entitlements: a monthly support amount, a shelter amount, and dozens of supplements for things like transportation, dental care or a special diet. Each can have its own rules, its own law behind it, and its own route to challenge a decision. Eligibility is whether a client qualifies for an entitlement, and from what date.

Fact (evidence)
A piece of information about a client that someone has claimed is true, such as their income.
In the new system a fact is never just a value like “$1,100”. It is a claim: who said it, what period it covers, and when the system learned it. The site mostly calls these claims evidence, because they are what a decision rests on. Where it says “fact”, it means a claim of this kind, never a bare value.
The Evidence page shows how this works, with a worked example.

Indigenous child
Under the CFCSA: a First Nation child, a Nisga'a child or a Treaty First Nation child; a child below the age the Act sets who has a biological parent of Indigenous ancestry, including Métis and Inuit, who considers themselves Indigenous; a child at or over that age who has Indigenous ancestry and considers themselves Indigenous; or a child an Indigenous governing body or Indigenous authority confirms, by advising a director, belongs to an Indigenous community.
Indigenous community
Used as each source uses it; no definition was found in the passages read. It is not the same as an Indigenous governing body or an Indigenous authority, and the duties owed to each differ. Has the meaning given in the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (CFCSA section 1). Interface
The agreed way one system asks another for information or asks it to do something.
An interface is like a published contract. It says what you can ask for, in what form, and what you get back. Other systems are built to rely on it, so it has to stay stable for a long time.

N12 In requirements: NFR-S-002 · DR-004
Lakehouse, analytics platform

In requirements: FR-096
Legacy assertion time
When the old system recorded a fact, for records moved from it.
Records moved from the old system all arrive in the new one on the same day. If that day were used as the date the ministry learned each fact, fifteen years of history would look as though it arrived at once. So each moved fact keeps a third date: when the old system recorded it. It carries a confidence marker, because the old record often cannot show it. Where the date is unknown, the system says so rather than guessing.
N01 asks for all three dates on every fact: valid time, transaction time and this one.

N01
Legal time limit
A deadline set in law or policy, such as the time the ministry has to decide.
Many steps in the ministry’s work have a deadline. A client has 20 business days to ask for a reconsideration. The ministry then has 10 business days to decide, or 20 with an approved extension. Some limits count business days and some count calendar days.
Missing some limits changes what the client is owed. That makes them part of the entitlement, not just a service standard, which is why N19 asks the system to track them.

N19 In requirements: FR-061 · INT-011
Limit on use
A rule that the ministry may hold a piece of information but not use it for a particular purpose.
Holding information lawfully is not the same as being allowed to use it for anything. Policy sometimes bars a use: a detail that must not count in a calculation, content that must not be shared with a certain party, a subject that must not be raised. N21 asks that the limit stays attached to the information, so it goes with every copy and the system can enforce it.

Permanent history (append-only store)
A store where new records are only ever added to the end, and nothing is overwritten.
Instead of changing a record in place, the system adds a new entry saying what changed. That keeps a full history, which is what lets a decision be replayed. But it clashes with the legal duty to destroy some records, and N12 exists to settle that clash before the first record is stored.
Used in:
[aria-label] N12: How records are destroyed is decided before anything is stored
N12
Permanent transfer of custody
A court order under the CFCSA, made before or after a continuing custody order, that makes a person other than the child's parent the child's guardian. It cannot be enforced, modified or cancelled under the Act and has the same effect as a guardianship order under the Family Law Act.
Plan of care
A plan relating to a child that contains the information required under the regulations and is prepared in accordance with them (CFCSA section 1). Policy and forms also call it a care plan.
Policy-as-code
Access rules written as versioned, testable code instead of settings changed by hand.
Post-adoption assistance
Assistance a director may provide under a written agreement after the adoption of a child the director has designated, on the income and asset tests the Adoption Regulation sets (FR-240).
Practice run (recovery exercise)
Deliberately taking a service down to prove it can be brought back within its targets.
A recovery plan that has never been tried is a guess. In a practice run the team simulates a failure, restores the service, and measures how long it took and how much data was lost. N16 counts a recovery target as real only once a practice run has met it.
Used in:
[aria-label] N16: Each service has recovery targets, proven in practice runs
N16
Practice-only
Said of a provision that rests on practice material alone (job aids, forms, user guides), with no legislation or policy held to support it. No requirement is written from it, and the missing authority is named.
Pre-decision communication
A message giving reasons and a response deadline, stating that no decision has been made yet. An aggregate of Eligibility & Entitlement, outside the pure function, carrying a no_decision_made marker (FR-006; ADR-004).
In requirements: FR-006
Prescribed class
A group of people the regulations treat as meeting disability designation without the usual application, often because another body has already assessed them.
In requirements: FR-030
Presentation hearing
The summary hearing held soon after a removal or an application for a supervision order, at which the court makes an interim order.
Prior contact check
A review of all previous records involving the individual who is the subject of the check, collected under the CFCSA or the Adoption Act. It starts only on that person's signed consent (FR-226).
Program policy authority
The ministry role responsible for a program's policy. It approves how rule outputs are classified and accepts what a rollback would lose.
In requirements: BR-014 · FR-003
Property guardian, personal guardian
Under a continuing custody order the director is the child's sole personal guardian and the Public Guardian and Trustee is the sole property guardian. During a temporary custody order the court may appoint the Public Guardian and Trustee property guardian.
In requirements: INT-035
Protected A, B, C
Canadian government security classifications for sensitive information, with C the most sensitive. Protected C may only be stored on-premise.
In requirements: NFR-P-006 · NFR-A-009 · NFR-C-001 · INT-001 · DR-003
Protection hearing
The hearing that follows the presentation hearing and decides whether the child needs protection. It ends or replaces the interim order.
Provision (CL-)
One thing that children and family services law or policy states, reconciled from two or more register rows and numbered CL-Dn-nnn. Each requirement in groups CF1 to CF18 lists the provisions it meets.
Pure evaluation
A calculation that uses only the inputs it is given, with no clock, database or network calls, so it gives the same answer every time.
In requirements: FR-090
PWD and PPMB
Persons with Disabilities designation and Persons with Persistent Multiple Barriers designation. Each gives access to higher rates or different rules.
RDSP, structured settlement
A Registered Disability Savings Plan; a structured settlement pays compensation in instalments. Both have special treatment in asset rules.
In requirements: FR-017
Reconsideration
A client’s first step to challenge a decision: asking the ministry to look at it again.
A reconsideration is done inside the ministry, by staff who had no part in the original decision. A client usually has 20 business days to ask for one. Some decisions cannot be reconsidered, and N20 asks the system to record which.
Used in:
[aria-label] N17: Different people decide, review and pay
N17 ·
[aria-label] N20: Each benefit records whether and how a decision can be challenged
N20
Reconsideration and Administrative Fairness Unit
The independent ministry unit that makes reconsideration decisions and decides whether reconsideration is available.
In requirements: BR-002 · BR-003 · FR-056 · INT-011
Recovery targets
How quickly a service must be back after a failure, and how much recent data it may lose.
There are two. The recovery time is how long the service may be down before it must be working again. The recovery point is how much recent work may be lost: a recovery point of one hour means at most the last hour of changes. Technical teams call these the RTO and the RPO.
For payments the architecture sets the recovery point at zero: no payment data may be lost at all.
Used in:
[aria-label] N16: Each service has recovery targets, proven in practice runs
N16 In requirements: NFR-A-002
Register row
One row of the children and family services register: an obligation (OB-), a rule (R-), a time limit (CK-), a record (RC-) or an authority (AU-), each pointing to the passage it came from. Ages, amounts and numbers of days are held in these rows and never stated in a requirement.
Regression corpus
A set of test cases with known answers that every rules change must still pass.
In requirements: FR-008 · FR-090
Release train
A fixed schedule of software releases that changes must wait for.
In requirements: NFR-A-002
Removal
A director's removal of a child without a court order, on reasonable grounds to believe that the child needs protection and that either the child's health or safety is in immediate danger or no available less disruptive measure is adequate to protect the child. A presentation hearing follows.
Repayable issuance
Money paid now against a signed promise to repay, which becomes a debt only if a later decision goes against the client. An aggregate of Financial Components, which decides nothing; interim assistance pending reconsideration or appeal is its principal instance (FR-041; ADR-005).
In requirements: FR-041
Replay
Running a past decision again, from its stored inputs, to show exactly how it was reached.
If a client appeals a decision made years ago, the ministry has to show what it decided and why. Replay means feeding the same rules and the same facts back through the same calculation, and getting exactly the same answer.
That only works if the calculation used nothing but its inputs (N07), and if every input was saved (N08).
