Given the Appeals & Reconsideration context, when its commands are inspected, then none can create or change an availability determination; it reads the DiscretionaryDetermination from Evidence & Verification.
Data
Inputs: the request and the adjudicability attributes. Outputs: the availability decision, as DiscretionaryDetermination evidence. Validations: the person deciding took no part in the original.
Dependencies
FR-036, FR-092
Rationale
If the context that runs reconsiderations also decided availability, it would rule on its own jurisdiction (NOTE-001 v2.0).

FR-059 Must M7 Medium
The tribunal is an outside party
The tribunal is an outside party listed in the integration inventory. Show detail
First needed in: M7
Description
The tribunal is an outside party listed in the integration inventory. For each appeal the system records how the appeal ended (decided, withdrawn or abandoned) separately from the panel's decision (confirmed or rescinded). It takes in the panel's decision as a decision made by an outside body. It records evidence that entered at the hearing with the hearing as its source. It carries out a rescission by making a new determination, never by editing the original. Amended 2026-09-30 (ADR-004 §5, ADR-006): v1.3 read "by cancelling the original decision and making a new one". A rescission never invalidates the original: the panel's rescinded determination is recorded as external-determination evidence with the tribunal (Employment and Assistance Appeal Tribunal; Notice of Appeal EAAT001) as its authority; the original determination record stands, annotated with the rescission reference; and the ministry re-determines as a retroactive determination consuming evidence whose provenance is the hearing. InvalidateEvidence is reserved for assertions that should never have existed. It keeps the ministry's representative separate from the original decision-maker and the reconsideration officer.
Relates To
BR-002, BR-003, UC-4
Obligations
OB-A05, OB-A06, OB-A07, OB-A09, OB-A14
Parameters
N01, N02, N08, N17
Acceptance Criteria
Given an appeal outcome, when it is recorded, then only the panel decisions the statute allows are available, and a withdrawn or abandoned appeal has no panel decision NOTE6-C1.
Given an appeal, when its outcome is recorded, then it has an appeal disposition (decided, withdrawn or abandoned), and only where the disposition is decided a panel determination (confirmed or rescinded). Reconsideration's own outcomes are a different attribute and are not unified with these (ADR-006).
Given a rescission, when it is recorded, then the original determination record still exists unchanged and carries an annotation with the rescission reference, and a work item to make the new retroactive determination is created. Amended 2026-09-30 (ADR-004 §5): v1.3 read "the original determination is cancelled without being replaced".
Given the choice of the ministry's representative at a hearing, when the candidate made or reconsidered the decision, then the assignment is refused.
Data
Inputs: tribunal decisions (INT-011). Outputs: appeal outcomes and outside decisions. Validations: only the statutory terms are allowed.
Dependencies
INT-011, FR-060
Rationale
The panel can only confirm or rescind, and it may consider evidence that is not in the record. If the list of outcomes is wider than the statute allows, people will use the extra options (NOTE-006).
FR-060 Must M7 High

When a client wins, the system makes a new retroactive determination and calculates the difference from the old one. Show detail
First needed in: M7

When a client wins, the system makes a new retroactive determination and calculates the difference from the old one. It then pays the underpayment or reverses the overpayment. (v1.3 read "an allowed appeal"; the panel's statutory terms are confirm and rescind, ADR-006.)
Given interim assistance paid pending the reconsideration or appeal, when the new determination issues, then the repayable issuance resolves on it (FR-041; ADR-005).
Given an underpayment to be put right, when it is calculated, then it is paid through the chokepoint with its purpose code.

H Statutory time 1
FR-061 Must M0 High
One register of legal time limits
Every statutory and policy time limit is registered once as a clock with a unique identifier. Show detail
First needed in: M0 (register), M7
Description
Every statutory and policy time limit is registered once as a clock with a unique identifier. Each clock records:
its owner (the ministry, the client, the tribunal or an outside adjudicator);
its class (entitlement or service standard);
the event that starts it, how long it runs, and its calendar base and day type;
the extensions allowed and who must authorise each.
The system detects and records a breach automatically. Where policy attaches a consequence, the system applies it without anyone asking. Business-day counting is one shared, tested capability.
Relates To
BR-003, UC-2, UC-4
Obligations
OB-R03, OB-R04, OB-R05, OB-R12, OB-A01, OB-A02, OB-A13
Parameters
N19, N01
Acceptance Criteria
Given the clock register, when it is loaded, then every clock states its owner, class, base and day type, with no defaults assumed. The obligation registers number clocks within each partition, and 18 of those numbers repeat across partitions; each clock gets a unique identifier instead.
Given a ministry-owned entitlement clock, when it is breached, then the breach is recorded and its effect on the effective date passes to FR-005 automatically.
Given a clock the ministry does not own, when it is breached, then the ministry bears no consequence for a breach it could not avoid.
Given day counting, when it is tested across holidays, year ends and February's shorter night counts, then every registered base counts correctly.
Data
Inputs: the provincial holiday calendar (reference data) and the start events. Outputs: running clocks and breach events. Validations: each clock is versioned and effective-dated like a rules artefact.
Dependencies
FR-090, FR-094
Rationale
Legal time limits are modelled once and used by every program TA-C21. A missed deadline changes what the client is owed PRIN-C1. Policy contains 138 clocks.
Added v1.6 (CK-LG1-41, R-LG1-119). Given a time limit that runs for every party to a court proceeding, the director among them, when it is registered, then the register names the owner as a party to the proceeding, and a party's missed limit is recorded without a consequence for the ministry unless the director was that party.
Added v1.6 (CL-D1-042, CL-D1-059, CL-D1-060). Given a time limit that policy states in hours, when it is registered, then the register holds the unit as hours and states whether the limit runs through evenings, weekends and holidays, with no default assumed.
Added v1.6 (CL-D1-041, CL-D1-052). Given a time limit whose length is agreed in the instrument itself within a registered maximum, when the clock starts, then it runs for the length recorded on that instrument, and the register holds the maximum and any default as data.
Added v1.6 (CL-D1-111). Given a clock that a statute suspends while a stated event lasts, when the event's start and end are recorded, then the clock stops for that period and resumes with the time it had left, and the suspension is shown on the clock's history.
Added v1.6 (CL-D1-123, CL-D1-127, CL-D1-130). Given a clock that counts back from a future event, such as a period of notice before a hearing, when the event's date is set or changed, then the system works out the last day to act, and a court direction that shortens, extends or dispenses with the period replaces it on that case.
Added v1.6 (CL-D1-142, CL-D1-143, CK-LG1-28). Given a clock counted back from a set date, such as a notice period before a hearing, when the date is set or changed, then the last day for the act is worked out again and the earlier result is kept as history.
Added v1.6 (CL-D1-141, CL-D1-142, CL-D1-146). Given a clock whose period an outside body may suspend, shorten, extend or dispense with, when that body's order is recorded, then the clock applies it and records the order as the authority.
Added v1.6 (CK-YJ5-16, CK-YJ5-17, CK-YJ5-20, CK-YJ5-21, CK-YJ5-22, CK-YJ5-23; conditional on DEP-28). Given a time limit that policy counts back from a scheduled event such as a hearing or a release date, when the clock is registered, then it records that direction, and when the event date changes, then the due date is worked out again and the change is recorded.
Added v1.6 (CK-YJ3-44, CK-YJ3-47, CK-YJ3-48, CK-YJ3-49, CK-YJ3-50, CK-YJ3-51; conditional on DEP-28). Given a time limit that policy states in minutes or hours, or one that recurs at an interval while an event continues, when it is registered, then the clock records its unit and its recurrence, runs at any hour without regard to business days, and records each interval that passes without the required act.

N Rules, adjudicability and automated decisions 5
FR-090 Must M0 High
Policy staff write rules as versioned, effective-dated artefacts
Eligibility rules, rates, clocks and reasons wording are versioned artefacts. Show detail
First needed in: M0 (minimum viable), M5
Description
Eligibility rules, rates, clocks and reasons wording are versioned artefacts. Each carries its policy citation and effective date. An embeddable engine runs them inside the determination service. Policy analysts write and simulate them. They are released through a pipeline with review, sign-off by two people and legal sign-off, and tested against a regression corpus that does not depend on any one engine. A change that reduces the corpus's coverage fails the pipeline.
Relates To
BR-001, BR-010, UC-7
Parameters
N04, N07, N01, N18
Acceptance Criteria
Given two named policy analysts working without help, when they write, simulate and release one real rate change end to end in a test environment, then it succeeds, and the time taken and help needed are recorded TA-C9.
Given a released artefact, when it is inspected, then it is fingerprinted and tagged, carries its policy citation and effective date, and has a regression result.
Given a released artefact, when its digest is computed, then the digest covers each rule's policy citation and effective-date marker, so the policy version is bound into every determination record as part of artefact 1. No separate policy artefact is bound (ADR-007).
Given a rule whose only authority is a spreadsheet, when someone tries to release it, then release is blocked until a policy citation exists or the rule is recorded as unauthorised for the ministry to decide.
Data
Inputs: policy text and rate tables. Outputs: rules artefacts. Validations: a citation and effective date are required.
Dependencies
D3 decision; FR-091
Rationale
Running the engine inside the service against a snapshot passed to it is what makes pure evaluation achievable (commitment 2). The business case for the rules platform is that rate changes no longer wait for a software release. That case assumes analysts can write rules in the tool, and nobody has tested that yet.

Parameters
N07, N05, N18
Acceptance Criteria
Given a comparison where two wrong components cancel out to the same total, when it runs, then it is reported as a difference TA-C26.
Given a timing difference, when one is seen, then it is raised as a defect in the snapshot mechanism, not sent for adjudication.
Given a difference in policy interpretation, when it is found, then it goes to the standing panel's queue, and the panel's ruling is built into the rules artefact.
Given the legacy side of the comparison, when it is set up, then it includes every legacy place the calculation happens (including MIS benefit calculation).
Data
Inputs: snapshots of legacy inputs and legacy decision records. Outputs: classified differences. Validations: difference records are classified and disposed of like any other client-affecting evidence.
Dependencies
FR-008, INT-023, DR-014
Rationale
Comparing live against a lagging copy makes timing the main source of differences. Replaying against recorded inputs removes timing by design (TA §C.2.7). The legacy output is the benchmark to compare against, not the specification.

FR-103 Must M6 High
Financial reconciliation between old and new systems, and the gate for moving payments
While old and new systems run side by side, a standing report compares them on money: Show detail
First needed in: M6
Description
While old and new systems run side by side, a standing report compares them on money: the total entitlement authorised and the total issued, for each program and each period, in both systems, reconciled to the ledger. Before payments for any group of clients move to the new system, the new system calculates in parallel and is reconciled to the corporate ledger. The variance must be zero, not within a tolerance, for three issuance cycles in a row. The Comptroller signs off. The emergency payment path has been exercised. The overpayment lifecycle has been shown from raising through to write-off and collections referral. Once payments have moved, the old payment path is switched off and its interfaces are closed.
Added v1.5.
Relates To
BR-004, BR-011, UC-6
Parameters
N14, N18, N05
Acceptance Criteria
Given both systems running, when the report is produced, then it shows authorised and issued totals by program and period for each system and the difference between them, and it is visible at deputy-minister level.
Given a proposal to move payments for a cohort, when any of the last three cycles shows a variance against the corporate ledger, then the gate fails TA-C49.
Given the gate, when it is held, then the record holds the Comptroller's sign-off, the report of the emergency path exercise (FR-047) and the end-to-end demonstration of the overpayment lifecycle.
Given a cohort whose payments have moved, when the gate is closed, then the old payment path for that cohort is off and its interfaces are closed, with evidence of both.
Given rows written back to the old system by the new one, when the report compares the two systems, then those rows are left out of both sides.
Data
Inputs: ledger totals from both systems; corporate ledger postings. Outputs: the reconciliation report; gate evidence. Validations: figures come from control totals, never from a sample.
Dependencies
FR-045, FR-047, FR-095, DR-014, INT-001
Rationale
Two documented failures in other jurisdictions had the same cause: payments were moved before they were reconciled. This is the figure an auditor will ask for (TA §E.5.6, §E.11.2).

CF1 Authority to act: delegation and approvals 6
This group covers who may act for a director: the record of each designation and delegation, the decisions to grant, limit, review and revoke a delegation, and the check that a delegation in force covers an act before it is recorded. It rests on the designation and delegation provisions of the CFCSA and the Adoption Act and on the ministry's delegation policy. It also holds the points at which policy requires a supervisor's approval.
FR-104 Must M0 Medium
A record of every designation of a director and every delegation
The system holds each designation of a director and each delegation of a director's powers, duties or functions as the record of a written instrument. Show detail
First needed in: M0 (schema), M9
Description
The system holds each designation of a director and each delegation of a director's powers, duties or functions as the record of a written instrument. The record states the Act it is made under, who made it, the person or class of person it is made to, the category or powers it covers, any terms or conditions, and the date it takes effect. Each later event on a delegation is added to the record with its date, and what was in force before stays readable. This record is the source the system uses to decide who may act for a director.
Relates To
BR-021
Service lines
Child protection and family services; guardianship; adoption and permanency; youth transitions; children and youth with support needs
Parameters
N01, N17, N04
Authority
CFCSA ss. 91, 91.1, 91.2 and 92; Adoption Act ss. 76.1 and 77; Delegation Handbook, Part C sections 5, 9 and 10 and Part D section 5 (CFD-134); Aboriginal Operational and Practice Standards and Indicators: Operational Standards, Appendix I (CFD-276) (tier 1)
Provisions
CL-D1-001, CL-D1-002, CL-D1-010, CL-D1-011, CL-D7-130, CL-D7-133, AU-LG1-01, AU-LG2-19, AU-LG2-21, OB-LG1-126, RC-LG2-11 (6 reconciled provisions and 5 further rows; 22 register rows in all)
Acceptance Criteria
Given a delegation, when it is entered, then the system refuses it unless it identifies the written instrument, the director who made it, the Act, the person or class of person, the category or powers, and any terms or conditions (OB-LG1-129, RC-LG2-12).
Given a delegation on record, when one of the events policy lists occurs (RC-CP1-01), then the event is added with its date and who recorded it, and every earlier state of the delegation can still be read as it stood.
Given a person found to be working without a delegation they should hold, when the delegation is entered, then the system refuses an effective date earlier than the date the delegation is made and requires a note that explains the delay (R-CP1-10, RC-CP1-04).
Edge case: a delegation is under review, limited or revoked. The person's record carries a brief pointer to the Designated Director that shows whatever category is later applied for, holds no detail of the concern, and is removed when it no longer applies (RC-CP1-02).
Given a designation of a director by the minister, when it is entered, then the record holds the written instrument, the provisions it is made for and any terms or conditions (OB-LG1-126, RC-LG2-11).
Data
Inputs: Written designations and delegations; delegation events; the note explaining a late delegation; Outputs: An effective-dated history of each person's delegation under each Act; Validations: Every state has a start date and a source instrument; no state starts before its instrument was made.
Dependencies
FR-004, FR-094, NFR-SEC-003
Open
Policy names a provincial database that tracks delegation. It is not on the list of systems being replaced. The ministry must decide whether the new system is the master of delegation records or receives them from that database.
The Delegation Handbook applies only to ministry Designated Directors and says it does not apply to Indigenous Child and Family Services Agencies. For agency employees the only source held is the 2009 operational standards, which name a First Nations Director of Child Welfare as delegator and a Delegation Registrar as administrator. Neither title is in the Act, which now provides for an Indigenous Child Welfare Director (s. 91.2). Who delegates to agency employees today must be confirmed.
CFCSA s. 92(1) and Adoption Act s. 77(1) are subject to the regulations. No regulation restricting delegation was read for this pack.
Adoption Act s. 77(3) requires a delegation of the Provincial director's Central Authority functions to accord with the Convention. The record holds the delegation; no source says what the system should check.
Rationale
Both Acts require a designation and a delegation to be in writing, with any terms or conditions (CFCSA ss. 91(2) and 92(2); Adoption Act ss. 76.1(2) and 77(2)). Policy requires each delegation event to be recorded and says authority cannot be given retroactively (CFD-134, Part C). A decision record can show its maker's authority only if that authority is held with its dates. LEG001-C1

The consultation and approval points come from the 2005 practice standards for delegated agencies. Policy describes those standards in the past tense (CFD-260) and their currency is unconfirmed (CL-D7-239).
For ministry workers the 2004 service standards name no approval levels and leave them to regions. Later policy chapters name the approver decision by decision; those approvals are written in the packs that hold each decision.
The child protection standard is headed as approval but its lists say the worker consults. The system records whichever the standard states at each point; the ministry should confirm which points need approval.
No source says whether a departure from a procedure is allowed outside the adoption policy.
Rationale
The adoption policy lets a worker depart from a Procedure only with the Team Leader's approval and a record of the reasons (CFD-277). The standards for delegated agencies require the supervisor's approval at key points so that the facts are reviewed before a decision is made (CFD-278). CFD277-C2
CF2 Indigenous identity, jurisdiction and agreements 33
This group covers an Indigenous child's identity and communities, whether an Indigenous law or an agreement applies, referral and transition to an Indigenous authority, notice before a significant measure, and the order of priority for placement. It rests on the Indigenous jurisdiction provisions of the CFCSA, the federal Act respecting First Nations, Inuit and Métis children, youth and families, and the ministry's policies on both. The requirements keep Indigenous governing body, Indigenous authority and Indigenous community apart, because the duties owed to each differ.
FR-110 Must M0 Medium
Confirming and recording whether a child is an Indigenous child, and each community
The system holds whether a child is an Indigenous child as a fact with its source, its date and the part of the statutory definition it rests on. Show detail
First needed in: M0 (schema), M9
Description
The system holds whether a child is an Indigenous child as a fact with its source, its date and the part of the statutory definition it rests on. It keeps 'not yet confirmed' apart from 'confirmed not Indigenous'. For an Indigenous child it records every Indigenous community the child belongs to, on the maternal and the paternal side, and the kind of community. For a child not identified as Indigenous it raises a renewed enquiry at the events policy lists.

Acceptance Criteria
Given a child with no recorded answer on Indigenous identity, when a worker starts work under the Act for that child, then the system shows identity as not yet confirmed, distinct from confirmed not Indigenous, and prompts the enquiry (OB-LG1-04).
Given a child is recorded as an Indigenous child, when the record is saved, then it holds the part of the statutory definition relied on (R-LG1-06, R-LG2-04), the source of the information, and each community on the maternal and paternal sides (RC-IN1-18).
Given an Indigenous child, when identity is recorded, then the record states whether the child belongs to a First Nation, the Nisga'a Nation or a Nisga'a Village, a Treaty First Nation, a Métis community or an Inuit region (RC-IN1-19).
Given a child not identified as Indigenous, when a parent or family member is newly identified, a change of placement or legal status is considered, the care plan is reviewed (CK-IN1-25) or an Indigenous community gives notice, then the system raises a renewed enquiry.
Edge case: an Indigenous governing body or Indigenous authority advises a director that the child belongs to an Indigenous community. The system records the child as an Indigenous child on that advice, with who advised and when (R-LG1-06).
Edge case: (practice only, to confirm) the system does not make documents proving status or membership a condition of recording a child's Indigenous identity (OB-IN4-52).

Open
The two Acts word the confirmation part of the definition differently: the CFCSA names an Indigenous governing body or Indigenous authority advising a director; the Adoption Act names an Indigenous community advising a director or an adoption agency. The record must say which Act's definition was applied.
A practice document (CFD-297) says identity is determined through self-identification. The Act also has membership, entitlement and confirmation, so the requirement follows the Act (CF-D7-09).
The rule against asking a family for documents rests on a practice document only (CFD-302). Policy 1.1 lists whom to ask and does not say what evidence may be required.
Policy 1.1 sets the renewed enquiry at care plan review 'at a minimum' interval and says the list of events is not exhaustive. No source sets a time limit for 'promptly'.
No information agreement under s. 28 of the federal Act is held, so whether the categories First Nations person, Inuk and Métis person must also be recorded is not settled.
Rationale
Section 4.3(1) of the Act requires a director to confirm promptly whether a child is an Indigenous child whenever the director acts under the Act. Every later duty in this group depends on that fact and on the communities recorded with it. LEG001-C3

Policy names a 'Repository' of agreements and laws and a table of Indigenous governing bodies and the communities they represent. Who owns that register and how it is kept current is not stated. The agreements themselves are specified in the agreements pack (P02b).

CL-D7-008, CL-D7-110, CL-D7-111, CL-D7-112, CL-D7-121, CL-D7-122, CL-D7-123, CL-D7-125, CL-D7-128, CL-D7-129, CL-D8-040, CL-D8-195, R-IN2-03 (12 reconciled provisions and 1 further rows; 41 register rows in all)
Acceptance Criteria
Given a community agreement made by one director, when any director or delegate in the province works with an Indigenous child of that community, then the agreement, its current version and its terms are available to them (R-LG1-124).
Edge case: a part of a community agreement under which the community provides services. The system does not apply that part province-wide or require information conditions for it (R-LG1-124, OB-LG1-130), and links it to the service contract that carries it.
Given an agreement of a kind the Act requires to carry conditions on the use, disclosure and security of information (OB-LG1-130, OB-LG1-122, OB-LG1-124, R-LG2-46), when it is recorded as in force without them, then the system refuses, unless the record names the regulation that exempts it.
Given an agreement whose terms set a duration, a review, a notice period for termination or a dispute resolution ladder (R-IN2-09, CK-IN2-03), when it is recorded, then those values are held on that agreement, its review and expiry dates raise work items, and no ministry-wide default is assumed.
Given any agreement, when it is recorded, then each party is recorded in its own right under the party type the Act names, including where several communities make one agreement together (R-IN2-03), with who signed for each party and in what capacity.
Data
Inputs: The signed agreement and each amendment; its kind and the provision it is made under; parties and signatories; purposes; terms; information conditions; effective, review and end dates; Outputs: A versioned agreement record that every director and delegate can read; review and expiry work items; the list of agreements in force for a community; Validations: The party type matches the kind of agreement; information conditions are present where the Act requires them; every version has an effective date.
Dependencies
FR-085, FR-084, FR-067, FR-074, FR-021
Open
The Community Agreements framework (CFD-046) is undated and its parent policy is not held. Its signing authorities and template terms (CL-D7-125, CL-D7-129) need the ministry to confirm they are current.
CFD-046 lists referral of child protection reports to a prescribed Nation as a fourth purpose of a community agreement. The consolidated Act shows s. 92.1(1) as repealed and s. 92.1(2) lists consultation and cooperation, services by the community and prescribed purposes only. The register follows the Act (CF-D7-04, read in both sources).
A regulation under CFCSA s. 103(2)(q.2) may exempt an agreement for a prescribed purpose from the information conditions and from applying to all directors. No such exemption was found in the Regulation as held.
No decision-making agreement, power or duty agreement or coordination agreement is held in the corpus, so the terms such agreements carry are known only from the Act.
Rationale
The Act makes an agreement a director makes with a community apply to all directors (CFCSA s. 92.1(4)), and policy requires a director to adhere to any such agreement (Policy 1.1). No director can do that unless every agreement and its terms can be found for the child in front of them. FR-085 holds data-sharing agreements as the source of access rights; these agreements also govern how assessments, plans and decisions are made. LEG001-C8
FR-118 Must M9 High
Applying the terms of an applicable agreement to work with an Indigenous child
The system finds the agreements that apply to an Indigenous child from the communities recorded for the child, and shows them wherever a director assesses, investigates, plans or decides for that child. Show detail
First needed in: M9
Description
The system finds the agreements that apply to an Indigenous child from the communities recorded for the child, and shows them wherever a director assesses, investigates, plans or decides for that child. Where a term of an agreement differs from a step, a time limit or an approval that policy sets, the system applies the agreement's term to that child's work and records that it did. Where the agreement sets how the community is involved, the system shows the term that fits the child's circumstances and records how it was met.

Acceptance Criteria
Given a child recorded as Indigenous, when a worker opens an assessment, an investigation, a plan or a placement decision for the child, then the system shows every agreement in force for every community the child belongs to, and the terms that cover that kind of work.
Given a term of an applicable agreement that conflicts with a step, time limit or approval that policy sets, when the system would apply the policy rule, then it applies the agreement's term to the extent of the conflict, and the decision record names the agreement, its version and the term applied (R-CP1-40, R-IN1-35).
Given a community agreement about family assessments or investigations (OB-LG1-28), when an assessment or investigation of an Indigenous child of that community is closed, then the record shows how each term of the agreement was met, or the reason it was not.
Given an agreement that sets different involvement for a child who lives near the community and one who lives far from it (R-IN2-08), when the child's place of residence is recorded or changes, then the system shows the term that fits and records which term was applied.
Edge case: the coordination agreement or Indigenous law named in an Indigenous authority's written confirmation cannot be found in the register. The system records this, routes the question to the team leader, and records any legal consultation and its result (AU-CP1-16).
Data

The sources state that an agreement prevails over policy. None read states that a community agreement displaces a time limit the Act itself sets. Terms of a decision-making or power or duty agreement that have the force of law are covered by FR-119.

FR-119 Must M0 High
Joint exercise and prior consent under a decision-making or power or duty agreement

Priority: MUST_HAVE (provisional: no agreement of this kind and no implementing policy is held)
First needed in: M0 (schema), M9
Description
Where a decision-making agreement or a power or duty agreement with an Indigenous governing body is in force, the system holds its terms on who exercises, performs or consents to each power, duty or statutory power of decision it covers, and its terms on criteria and procedures. It routes each exercise of a covered power to the persons the agreement identifies. It does not let the exercise be completed until the joint exercise or the consent the agreement requires is recorded. It keeps each power or duty agreement and each amendment with the date it was published.

Acceptance Criteria
Given an agreement that requires the consent of an Indigenous governing body before a director's power is exercised or a director's duty is performed, when a director tries to complete that exercise for a matter the agreement covers, then the system refuses until the consent, the person who gave it and its date are recorded.
Given an agreement that requires a power or duty to be exercised jointly, when the decision is recorded, then the decision record names each person who exercised it and the agreement and version relied on, and keeps each person's reasons as their own.
Given criteria or procedures the agreement sets for a covered power, duty or statutory power of decision (R-LG1-120), when it is exercised, then the system applies them and the decision record shows them as the rules applied.
Given a power or duty agreement or an amendment to one, when it is recorded as in force, then the system holds the copy for publication and the date it was published, and reports any agreement or amendment with no publication recorded (OB-LG1-121, OB-LG2-41).
Edge case: a power, duty or statutory power of decision under the Adoption Act that an agreement covers (OB-LG2-42). The same routing, consent and record apply.

Acceptance Criteria
Given an agreement in force that provides for the list, when the interval the agreement sets comes due (CK-IN2-01), then the system produces the list of the community's Indigenous children whose care status the Regulation describes (RC-LG2-36) and raises a work item for the director who discloses it.

Dependencies
FR-077, FR-080, FR-085, FR-061, FR-067
Open
The Regulation says 'on a regular basis'. CFD-046, which is undated, says quarterly. The interval is held on each agreement (CK-IN2-01).
CFD-046 describes the children listed as those in care or in the interim or temporary custody of a person other than a parent under a director's supervision. The Regulation describes them as children in care and children who are the subject of an interim order for custody or a temporary custody order. The requirement follows the Regulation.
CFD-046 names 'the director' in one place and a named deputy director in another as the person who discloses the list. The source check found this is not a conflict (CF-D7-23). The role that discloses is held as reference data.
No source says how a child who belongs to more than one community is listed, or what happens where a parent or youth objects. CFD-046 says an agreement may add steps for an objection.
The framework's diagrams of roles in completing and maintaining an information agreement were images and are not in the text held.
Rationale
The Regulation prescribes this purpose so that a community can fulfil its shared responsibility for the upbringing and well-being of its children, and fixes what the list may hold (CFCS Regulation s. 12.1(a)). The Act requires the agreement to carry conditions on the information provided (CFCSA s. 92.1(3)). The list must be produced from case records, on time, with no more than the Regulation allows. FR-121 Should M9 Medium
Requests for agreements, and the date an Indigenous law takes force by agreement or lapse of time
The system records a notice from an Indigenous governing body that an Indigenous group, community or people intends to exercise its legislative authority over child and family services, and a request for a coordination agreement, each with the day it was made. Show detail
Priority: SHOULD_HAVE (no implementing policy held; negotiation may be tracked outside the case system)
First needed in: M9
Description
The system records a notice from an Indigenous governing body that an Indigenous group, community or people intends to exercise its legislative authority over child and family services, and a request for a coordination agreement, each with the day it was made. It runs the period the federal Act sets from the day of the request and records whether a coordination agreement was entered into. BR-016
Service lines

Authority
An Act respecting First Nations, Inuit and Metis children, youth and families (federal) ss. 20(1) to (7), 21 and 22; CFCSA ss. 90.1(1), 90.2 and 90.4 to 90.6 (tier 1)
Provisions
CL-D7-111, CL-D7-114, CL-D7-117, AU-LG3-01, AU-LG3-02, CK-LG3-01, R-LG3-12 (3 reconciled provisions and 4 further rows; 10 register rows in all)
Acceptance Criteria
Given a request from an Indigenous governing body for a coordination agreement, when the day the request was made is recorded, then the system starts the period the federal Act sets (CK-LG3-01) as a registered time limit and shows the day after it ends.
Given the period ends with no coordination agreement entered into, when that day is reached, then the system raises a work item for a recorded finding on whether the conditions of the federal Act are met (R-LG3-12), and shows the law as having force from the day after the period ends only once that finding is recorded.
Edge case: a coordination agreement entered into after the period ends, or a new request. The system records each and keeps the earlier request and its outcome.
Given a request from the Nisga'a Nation or a Treaty First Nation for an agreement on law-making outside its lands (OB-LG1-125), when it is recorded, then the system keeps the efforts made to negotiate and their dates against the request.
Given an amending agreement or an enabling agreement, when it is recorded, then the system records each condition the Act sets for it (R-LG1-121) and shows the law as applying outside the Nation's lands only from the date the Act gives, once every condition is recorded as met.
Data
Inputs: The notice and the request, each with the day it was made and the Indigenous governing body that made it; the group, community or people it acts for; negotiation events; the agreement and the conditions met; Outputs: A running period with its end date; a work item at the end of the period; the date from which a law has force, passed to the record of applicable Indigenous law; Validations: The start day is the day the request was made; a law is shown as in force only on a recorded agreement or a recorded finding.
Dependencies
FR-061, FR-067, FR-085, FR-021
Open
No policy or procedure was found for receiving a notice or a request under the federal Act s. 20, or a request under CFCSA s. 90.4. Who in government receives them, and whether the ministry's case system or another body's records hold them, needs a ministry answer.
The federal Act does not say who finds that an Indigenous governing body made reasonable efforts. The requirement records the finding and does not make it.
CFCSA s. 90.4 sets no time limit for negotiation, so the requirement runs none.
Pack P02a holds the record of which Indigenous law applies to a child. This requirement supplies dates to it and should be read with it.
Rationale
Under the federal Act an Indigenous law gains the force of federal law either when a coordination agreement is entered into or when a set period passes after a request with reasonable efforts made (s. 20(3) and (4)). The Act gives the Nisga'a Nation and Treaty First Nations a parallel route by agreement (CFCSA ss. 90.5 and 90.6). Which law applies to a child turns on these dates, so the system must hold them. Given an Indigenous child, when the decision is recorded, then it shows the consideration of placing the child with or near children of the same parent or other family, and the consultation with the family and Indigenous community, including on customary care or custom adoption (OB-LG3-11, OB-LG3-12, OB-IN1-65).
Given a child who is not Indigenous, when the decision is recorded, then it shows placement with a relative or, failing that, which of the considerations the Act lists the placement meets (OB-LG1-115).
Given a placement for which policy names an approver, when no approval is recorded, then the system does not record the child as placed. This covers a permanent transfer of custody to a care provider who is neither family nor Indigenous (AU-CP2-02) and the cases in AU-AD1-06 and AU-IN3-03.
Edge case: an arrangement under the Extended Family Program, or a transfer of custody that follows one. Chapter 4 treats the placement priorities as not applicable (R-CP2-23), and the system does not require a priority record.
Edge case: a child in care is placed with a parent who is not apparently entitled to custody. The system records a placement with a parent, linked to the restricted caregiver agreement and the assessment policy requires (R-IN1-46), and does not record a return.
Data
Inputs: The child's recorded Indigenous identity and communities; parents, family members and their relationship to the child; the proposed care provider and how the provider relates to the child and community; the applicable order of priority; Outputs: A placement decision record with the step met, reasons for steps passed over, considerations and consultations; an approval where one is required; Validations: The order used is the one in force for the child and the kind of placement on the decision date; a placement that needs approval is not recorded as made without it.
Dependencies
FR-001, FR-004, FR-094
Open
MQ-023 (CF-D2-03, CF-D7-02): two statutes give different orders for an Indigenous child. The federal Act starts with a parent; CFCSA s. 71(3) starts with extended family or the child's Indigenous community. Both are held as reference data and neither is preferred here.
CF-D2-02, read in the source: the Adoption Policy of November 2022 matches under the CFCSA order with a team leader's approval to move to the general considerations, while Policy 1.1 and the Permanency Policies apply the federal order. Both are T2. Which applies to adoption matching waits on MQ-023.
The Aboriginal Operational and Practice Standards and Indicators date from 2005 and their currency is unconfirmed. Their rule that a supervisor approves a placement outside the child's community (R-IN3-21, AU-IN3-03) is held as approval data and should be confirmed for agencies.
The questions and answers say the priorities also apply to voluntary care and special needs agreements and to adoption requests (R-IN4-52). No policy held says so for those agreements.
Resource Work Policy 8.2, which governs the assessment of a restricted caregiver, is not held. Who counts as the parent after an adoption or a permanent transfer of custody rests on the questions and answers only (R-IN4-54).
The care plan form records placement against the CFCSA priorities only (R-GU1-43, R-GU1-40). It is practice material and is not followed where it differs from the Act.
Rationale
The federal Act sets an order of priority for placing an Indigenous child, to the extent consistent with the child's best interests (s. 16(1)), and the CFCSA sets the priority for other children (s. 71(2)). A placement outside the order must be explained by the child's best interests, and policy reserves some of those placements for a named approver. LEG005-C5

CF3 Reports, screening and the protection response 18
This group covers a report that a child needs protection, from receipt and screening through the family development response or investigation to ongoing protection services and their end. It rests on the duty to report and the director's duty to assess in the CFCSA, and on the Child Protection Response Policies.
FR-143 Must M0 Medium
Receiving and recording a report that a child needs protection
The system records every report that a child needs protection as a record of its own, from any person, on any channel and at any hour, with the date and time it was received. Show detail
First needed in: M0 (schema), M9
Description
The system records every report that a child needs protection as a record of its own, from any person, on any channel and at any hour, with the date and time it was received. It holds the information policy lists to be obtained from the reporter, each item with its source. It tells a new report apart from further information on a matter already open. It links a new report to a protection response already open for the same family unless a supervisor decides otherwise.

Acceptance Criteria
Given a person who reports that a child may need protection, when a worker records the report, then the system stores the date and time received, which start the time limits in FR-144 and FR-145, and holds each item policy lists (OB-CP4-01), marking any item the reporter could not give as not obtained.
Edge case: the reporter gives no name, or says the information is privileged or is confidential under another Act (R-LG1-38). The system accepts and records the report all the same and does not require the reporter's identity (OB-IN1-24).
Given information received about a family with an open case, when the worker records it, then the worker classifies it as a new report under the tests policy sets (R-CP4-01) or as information for the assigned office. Information that is not a new report goes to the assigned office and starts no screening time limit.
Given a new report received while a protection response to earlier concerns is open, when the assigned worker records it, then the system links the report to the open response, unless a supervisor records a decision to treat it separately, with the reason (AU-CP4-02).

Open

Policy says to consult a supervisor where it is unclear whether information is a new report (CFD-261 L303). It does not say the consultation must be recorded.
Acceptance of anonymous reports is stated only in the 2005 standards for delegated agencies (CFD-278), whose currency is unconfirmed. Chapter 3 asks for the reporter's name 'as much as possible'.
Rationale

Given a child protection response, when the worker records a reasonable likelihood that domestic violence is a factor (R-CP1-61), then the system opens the summary of domestic violence risk factors for the assigned worker and holds the completed summary as evidence (OB-CP1-82).

Given a registry result, when it is recorded, then it is held as evidence with its source and date. Where it directly affects case direction or a decision, the system requires a recorded verification from one of the bodies policy names before the decision relies on it (R-CP4-10).
Edge case: the child or youth is Indigenous. The steps on whether a coordination agreement or Indigenous law applies come before the check, and the system records the order.
Data

For each parent of the child it records the director's opinion on each criterion the Act sets, and it does not record an agreement as made unless the director and every parent who meets all the criteria are parties or, where no parent meets them, the first alternative the Act names. For an Indigenous child it records which body is included as a party, that body's role, and the conditions on the use, disclosure and security of the information the body is given.
Relates To
BR-017
Service lines
Child protection and family services
Parameters
N13, N17, N21
Authority
CFCSA ss. 19.2, 19.3(1)(b) and (c) and 19.9(1); Child Protection Response Policies (CFD-261), Policies 3.1, 3.2 and 3.3, 'Necessary Parties to a Safety Plan Agreement' and 'Other Parties'; Policy 1.1 Working with Indigenous Children, Youth, Families and Communities (CFD-301), section 3(b); Practice Directive on domestic violence (CFD-265), sections 5 and 6 (tier 1)
Provisions
CL-D1-043, CL-D1-045, CL-D1-046, CL-D1-047, CL-D1-058, CL-D1-062, OB-CP4-14, RC-CP4-08 (6 reconciled provisions and 2 further rows; 21 register rows in all)
Acceptance Criteria
Given the parents recorded for a child, when a worker prepares an agreement, then the system requires the director's opinion, with reasons, on each criterion the Act sets for each parent: apparently entitled to custody; has a parent's rights and responsibilities that the agreement may affect; can be located; able and willing to exercise them. Where a parent cannot be located, the reasons include the efforts made to locate the parent. The system does not record the agreement as made unless the director and every parent who meets all the criteria are parties (R-LG1-44, RC-CP4-08).
Given no parent meets all the criteria, when the agreement is made, then the system requires as a party the first that applies of: a parent who meets them all except that the agreement does not affect that parent's rights or responsibilities; a parent with care of the child (R-LG1-44, R-CP4-13).
Given a person or body the Act permits to be included as a party, when a necessary party does not agree to their inclusion, then the system does not add them. Where only another optional party objects, the necessary parties may go ahead without one or both optional parties. The persons permitted are a person with a right of contact or access under a court order or an agreement enforceable under the Family Law Act, and a parent who is not a necessary party (R-LG1-45, R-CP4-16).
Given an Indigenous child, when a body is included as a party, then the system accepts only the body the Act names for that child (the First Nation; the Nisg̱a'a Nation or the child's Nisg̱a'a Village; the Treaty First Nation; or the legal entity representing the child's Indigenous community), records the parents' consent, and requires that party's role and the conditions on the use, disclosure and security of the information it is given. It attaches those conditions to the record of everything disclosed to that party under the agreement (R-LG1-16, RC-LG1-06, R-IN1-44).
Given a person who could be a necessary party is located after a verbal agreement is made, when that is recorded, then the system creates a work item to establish whether the person agrees to the existing terms, and records the outcome: the parties end the agreement and make a new one that includes the person, or the director withdraws and a new agreement or another measure follows (OB-CP4-14).
Edge case: a separate agreement may be made with each parent, or with one parent alone, only where its terms do not affect the other parent's rights and responsibilities. The system records the director's opinion on that point and gives copies of each agreement only to its own parties (R-CP4-18, R-CP1-64).
Edge case: a parent or other permitted person who is still a child under the Act (R-LG1-45) may be a party in their own right, and the agreement is effective for that person.
Data
Inputs: The parents recorded for the child; court orders and Family Law Act agreements on custody, contact and access; the child's Indigenous identity and community; the director's opinion on each criterion; each necessary party's agreement to an optional party; Outputs: A party record for each party: role, whether necessary or optional, and basis; the director's recorded opinions; for an Indigenous party, its role and information conditions; Validations: The director and every parent who meets all the criteria are parties; no optional party is added over a necessary party's objection; an Indigenous party has a role and information conditions recorded.
Dependencies
FR-004, FR-077, FR-080, FR-084, FR-085, FR-089, DR-005
Open
CF-D1-04: Policies 3.2 and 3.3 and the domestic violence directive say a parent barred from access by an order may be omitted or need not be involved. Policy 3.1 keeps that parent in where the agreement affects parental responsibilities beyond parenting time. The Act makes a party of every parent who meets its criteria, so the requirement records the director's opinion on each criterion and treats no order as an automatic exclusion.
CF-D1-06: Policy 3.3 prints a second, older block of necessary-party text ('has custody'; 'all necessary parties'). The requirement follows the Act and the first block.
The agreement form (practice material) applies the information conditions for an Indigenous party only when a box is ticked. The Act requires them whenever such a party is included, and the requirement follows the Act.
Neither the Act nor policy sets out the conditions themselves. The agreement form's appendix carries a standard set: confidentiality that continues after the agreement ends, use only for the party's role, safeguards, and telling the worker at once if privacy may be at risk. Whether that set is required is to be confirmed.
Policy describes the located-parent procedure for a verbal agreement only. The Act lets the director withdraw from any agreement that no longer reflects who should or could be a party (s. 19.5(2)(c)).
Rationale
The Act names who must and who may be a party and rests the test on the director's opinion (CFCSA s. 19.2). It requires every party's role, and for an Indigenous party the conditions on the information it is given, to be in the agreement (s. 19.3(1)(b) and (c)). Whose withdrawal ends the agreement depends on the basis on which each person is a party (s. 19.7(1)), so that basis must be on the record from the start. LEG001-C30
FR-165 Must M9 Medium
Leaving a parent out of a safety plan agreement: rationale, approval, re-engagement
The system records a decision to leave a parent out of a safety plan agreement because, in the director's opinion, the parent is temporarily unable to exercise a parent's rights and responsibilities. Show detail
Priority: MUST_HAVE (who is re-engaged waits on MQ-006)

Description
The system records a decision to leave a parent out of a safety plan agreement because, in the director's opinion, the parent is temporarily unable to exercise a parent's rights and responsibilities. It requires the circumstance relied on and the rationale, and sends the decision for approval to the Director of Operations, or the equivalent position in an Indigenous Child and Family Services Agency, within the time limit policy sets. It starts the time limit for re-engaging the parent and reassessing the parent's ability, and closes that limit early where a court order that defines the parent's involvement is recorded.

Acceptance Criteria
Given a parent who would otherwise be a necessary party, when a worker records that the parent is left out as temporarily unable to exercise a parent's rights and responsibilities, then the system requires the circumstance relied on and the rationale as the reasons for the director's opinion, and records whether the team leader was consulted (RC-CP4-09, R-CP4-19).
Given such a decision, when it is recorded, then the system creates an approval item for the Director of Operations, or the equivalent position in an Indigenous Child and Family Services Agency, due within the time limit policy sets (CK-CP4-11), and records the approval or refusal, who gave it and when. Where no approval is recorded within the limit, the system records the breach and shows it to the supervisor (AU-CP4-08).
Given such a decision, when it is recorded, then the system starts the re-engagement limit (CK-CP4-12) and creates a work item to re-engage the parent left out and reassess that parent's ability to exercise a parent's rights and responsibilities. The worker records who was re-engaged and the outcome: the parent enters an agreement, or the parent remains unable, with reasons (OB-CP4-15, OB-CP1-85).
Edge case: where a court order that defines the parent's involvement is recorded before the re-engagement limit ends, the system closes the re-engagement item with that reason (CK-CP4-12, CK-CP1-42).
Edge case: where the parent remains unable, the system lets an agreement continue with the able parent and keeps the omission open for follow-up, so that a recorded change in the parent's circumstances prompts a new reassessment (OB-CP4-15).

Open

Policies 3.2 and 3.3 and the directive rest it on the worker's own opinion and re-engage only the parent left out. All are policy, so the requirement records both points and waits for the ministry's answer.
Policy does not say what follows if approval is refused or is not obtained within the limit.
The limits are stated in hours. No source says whether they run through evenings, weekends and holidays.
The approval and re-engagement rules are printed only under the 'temporarily unable' ground. The directive ties the approval to omission under s. 19.2(1)(b)(iv), which also covers a parent who is unwilling. Whether the rules apply when a parent is left out for another reason is to be confirmed.
Rationale
Policy lets a parent be left out only for the immediate term and requires a documented rationale, approval by the Director of Operations and re-engagement, each within a set limit (Child Protection Response Policies, Policy 3.1; practice directive on domestic violence, section 6.3). The Act makes a party of every parent who is able and willing (CFCSA s. 19.2(1)(b)(iv)), so each omission needs a record that can be reviewed. CFD261-C15
FR-166 Must M9 Medium
Making a safety plan agreement: legal advice, verbal agreements and written confirmation
The system supports making a safety plan agreement verbally or in writing. Show detail
First needed in: M9
Description
The system supports making a safety plan agreement verbally or in writing. Before an agreement is recorded as made, it requires a record that each party was told they may seek independent legal advice at any time with respect to the agreement. It treats the agreement as effective from the date all parties agreed, whether or not anyone has signed. For an agreement made verbally it tracks the written copy, the copy given to each party, and each party's signature or written confirmation, and it applies policy's conditions on a verbal agreement made without face-to-face contact.

Acceptance Criteria
Given a proposed agreement, when a worker tries to record it as made, then the system requires, for each party, a record of when and by whom the party was told they may seek independent legal advice at any time with respect to the agreement, and keeps that statement with the agreement (OB-LG1-33, RC-CP4-11).
Given all parties have agreed to the terms, when the agreement is recorded, then its start date is the date on which the last party agreed, whether the agreement was verbal or written and whether or not anyone has signed. A written copy prepared later carries the same start date (R-LG1-48, R-CP4-21).
Given a verbal agreement made because face-to-face contact with the parents was not possible, when it is recorded, then the system requires the exceptional circumstance and the team leader's approval, proposes the default term policy gives (R-CP4-12), requires consultation with the team leader and the necessary parties' agreement for a longer term, and starts the limit for following up face to face (CK-CP4-06, AU-CP4-06).
Given an agreement made verbally, when it is recorded, then the system creates work items to prepare the written copy, to give a copy to each party, and to obtain each party's signature or written confirmation that the written terms reflect what the party agreed to. Each is marked as soon as practicable, the efforts made are recorded, and a confirmation by electronic signature, email or text message is filed with the agreement (OB-LG1-34, RC-LG1-08, RC-CP4-07).
Given a party's signature cannot be obtained, when the worker records that, then the system requires the rationale and keeps the request for written confirmation open. The agreement stays in effect (OB-CP4-33, R-LG1-48).
Given any party or proposed party, when an agreement is being made, then the system shows that party's recorded communication needs to the worker and records how the director communicated with the party, that the party understood the terms and that the party agreed voluntarily (OB-LG1-39, OB-CP4-32).

Open
CF-D1-05: the Act says a parent may seek legal advice 'at any time with respect to the agreement'. The policy sentences say 'at any time after entering into' the agreement, though the same policy's record lists say 'at any time'. The requirement uses the Act's words.
The Act requires the information for each parent proposed as a party; policy requires it for every party. The requirement follows policy, which asks for more.
Policy 3.1 ties team leader approval, the default term and the follow-up limit to a verbal agreement made when face-to-face contact is not possible. Policies 3.2 and 3.3 say only that an agreement 'may be made verbally'. The requirement applies the Policy 3.1 conditions to that case alone; the ministry should confirm.
No source says whether the follow-up limit (CK-CP4-06) is counted in calendar or business days.
Policy has a verbal agreement written up in the case record and again on the written agreement, and names neither as the record. The requirement keeps one agreement record with its written copy.
Legal advice is needed on the kind of signature this instrument requires (FR-074). Policy accepts confirmation by email or text message, and FR-027 refuses a signature where identity is not verified to the registered level.
Rationale
The Act makes an agreement effective on the date all parties agree, whether or not anyone signs (CFCSA s. 19.4(4)). It requires the director to tell each parent about independent legal advice beforehand, and to follow up with a written copy and a signature or written confirmation as soon as practicable (s. 19.4(2) and (3)). The record must therefore hold the true effective date and the follow-up as separate facts. LEG001-C31
FR-167 Must M9 Medium
Withdrawal from a safety plan agreement, notice to the parties and termination
The system records every withdrawal from a safety plan agreement: Show detail
First needed in: M9
Description
The system records every withdrawal from a safety plan agreement: who withdrew, when, whether verbally or in writing, and why. It works out from the party's basis whether the withdrawal terminates the agreement, and records the agreement as terminated on the earliest of the dates the Act names. It requires the director's withdrawal when the assessment or investigation has concluded and no court application is pending, and records the ground for any other withdrawal by the director. It tracks the director's duty to tell each party of the withdrawal and to give the reasons to each parent who is a necessary party.

Child protection and family services
Parameters

Authority

Provisions
CL-D1-041, CL-D1-045, CL-D1-052, CL-D1-053, CL-D1-054, CL-D1-055, CL-D1-056 (7 reconciled provisions and 0 further rows; 32 register rows in all)
Acceptance Criteria
Given a party other than the director tells the director they will withdraw, when that is recorded, then the system records the date the director was informed, the date of withdrawal, whether it was verbal or in writing, the reasons, and whether the number of days' notice stated in the agreement was given (OB-LG1-38, CK-LG1-09, RC-CP4-10).
Given an agreement in force, when the earliest of these is reached: withdrawal by the director or by a parent who is a necessary party; a date agreed by all parties; the end of the term, then the system records the agreement as terminated on that date and which of them ended it. A withdrawal by any other party does not terminate the agreement, which continues for the remaining parties (R-LG1-50, R-CP4-23).
Given an agreement in force and an assessment or investigation that has concluded, when any of these is recorded: the director is not applying for an order to protect the child; the director withdraws the application; the court decides the application, then the system requires the director's withdrawal from the agreement to be recorded (OB-LG1-35, R-CP4-25).
Given a withdrawal by the director in any other case, when it is recorded, then the system requires the date and the ground the Act names: the agreement is no longer necessary; it is not adequate; it does not reflect a change in who should or could be a party or in the custody of the child; or it does not reflect a change in a person's willingness or ability to act as a parent with custody, or in a right of contact or access (R-LG1-49).
Given the director is withdrawing, when the withdrawal is recorded, then the system asks whether telling a party in advance could put the child's health or safety at risk and, where it could, sends that party no advance notice. It creates items to inform each party of the withdrawal as soon as practicable where the party was not told in advance, and to give the reasons to each parent who is a necessary party, and records when each was done (OB-LG1-36, OB-LG1-37, OB-CP4-36).
Given any party withdraws, when the withdrawal is recorded, then the system creates a work item to reassess whether a new agreement or another step under the Act is needed (R-CP4-17, R-CP4-23).
Edge case: an agreement in force never stops the system recording any other step the Act authorises to protect the child (R-LG1-52).
Data
Inputs: Withdrawals and notices of withdrawal with dates, form and reasons; each party's basis; the agreement's notice days and term; the state of the assessment or investigation and of any court application; the director's decision on advance notice; Outputs: Withdrawal records; the termination date and cause; items to inform parties and to give reasons; reassessment work items; Validations: Only a necessary party's withdrawal, all parties' agreement or the end of the term terminates an agreement; a discretionary withdrawal by the director names a ground the Act lists; no advance notice goes to a party where the director's decision bars it.
Dependencies
FR-061, FR-064, FR-067, FR-080, FR-089
Open
The Act does not say what follows when a party withdraws without giving the agreed notice.
No source says whether the notice days are calendar days; the agreement form (practice material) says calendar days.
The director's withdrawal when a report is referred to an Indigenous authority is held by pack P03a (CL-D1-065) and is not restated here.
Rationale
The Act fixes when an agreement terminates and whose withdrawal ends it (CFCSA ss. 19.6 and 19.7). It obliges the director to withdraw once the assessment or investigation is over and no application is pending (s. 19.5(1)), and bars advance notice of the director's withdrawal where it could put the child at risk (s. 19.5(3)). The system must hold these as rules so that an agreement is never shown as in force after the law has ended it. LEG001-C32

Given a special needs agreement, when it is sent for approval, then the system requires the assessment by a qualified professional, the assessment of the parents' ability to care, their review with a supervisor or team leader, and the parents' signed acknowledgement letter.
Edge case: Given a child who disagrees after a private discussion, when the worker records that, then the system requires a recorded consultation with a supervisor or team leader on alternatives, as policy sets by the child's age (OB-CP2-54).
Edge case: Given a dependent child of a child in care, when the only recorded reason for a voluntary care agreement is medical support, then the system does not let the agreement proceed (R-CP2-56).
Data
Inputs: Custody evidence, the child's views, alternatives considered, best interests reasoning, professional assessment, parents' acknowledgement letter; Outputs: A record of the considerations, fixed at the time the agreement is approved; Validations: The agreement type decides which considerations are mandatory; a consideration marked not possible needs a reason.
Dependencies
FR-004, FR-071, FR-074
Open
The Act does not define special needs. Policy 2.4 does (R-CP2-66) and also allows parental information with consent to an assessment in place of a completed assessment; the ministry should confirm which evidence is enough.
Policy 2.4 says a special needs agreement should not be used where the child must live away from home because of a child protection concern; how that is recorded is left to the protection response requirements.
Rationale
Section 6(3) and (4) of the Act, applied to special needs agreements by section 7(3), make these considerations a condition of the agreement. Policy 2.4 requires an objective professional assessment before a special needs agreement. LEG001-C34

CL-D1-109, CL-D1-110, CL-D1-111, CL-D1-115, OB-CP1-21, R-CP1-18, R-LG1-66, RC-LG1-09 (4 reconciled provisions and 4 further rows; 18 register rows in all)
Acceptance Criteria
Given a plan presented for approval, when the child is at or over the age the Act sets (OB-LG1-40), then the system refuses approval until it holds a record that the plan was explained to the child and a record of the child's views.
Given a plan, when a supervisor approves it, then the approval is recorded as the director's consent, with the participants who agreed and who receives a copy. When it is not approved, the record holds the changes required or the reasons the process is abandoned (AU-CP1-07).
Given a family conference plan of care, when its term or an extension is entered, then the system refuses a period, or a total across all consecutive plans for the child with all directors, beyond the Act's limits (CK-LG1-10), and requires the agreement of the director and of those who developed the plan.
Given a proceeding adjourned so that a collaborative process can go ahead, when the adjournment is recorded, then every time limit that applies to the proceeding stops running until it ends, the total adjourned time is tracked against the Act's limit (CK-LG1-11), and any written agreement the director files with the court is recorded as filed.
Given an approved plan, when it is in effect, then the system holds the plan's timelines as dated commitments and records each review of the plan with what the review found (OB-CP1-21).
Edge case: the child's immediate safety is at risk while a plan is in effect. The system accepts protective action, including a removal, at once. No step of the plan's back-up plan or dispute resolution process is a precondition (R-CP1-18, R-LG1-66).
Data
Inputs: The plan and its terms; the participants and their agreement; the child's date of birth and views; the supervisor's decision; the court's adjournment order; the limits on term (CK-LG1-10, CK-LG1-11); Outputs: An approved or not-approved plan with its term; review records; suspended and resumed time limits on the proceeding; a record of filing with the court; Validations: No approval without the child's views where the Act requires them; no term or total beyond the Act's limits; time limits resume when the adjournment ends.
Dependencies
FR-004, FR-061, FR-067, FR-074
Open
The Act's limits on term apply to a plan of care developed by means of a family conference. No source says whether an agreement from mediation or another process has a limit on its term.
The Act requires the director's consent. Policy has the worker and supervisor settle beforehand what level and scope of consent the attending worker may give, and has the supervisor approve the finished plan. No source says whether consent given at the conference within that scope is the director's consent, or only the supervisor's later approval.
Policy asks for 'timely' approval and sets no time limit. Policy sets no interval for reviewing a plan after approval.
The Act counts the plan's term and the adjournment in months and does not say how a part month is counted.
Rationale
The Act requires a family conference plan of care to include the director's consent, requires the plan to be explained to an older child before the director agrees, and limits the plan's term and the total of consecutive plans (CFCSA s. 21). It suspends any time limit applicable to a proceeding adjourned for a collaborative process (s. 23). Policy places approval with the supervisor and requires the plan to be reviewed after approval (Policy 3.4). LEG001-C40

The federal Act does not say how or to whom the reasonable efforts are demonstrated. Policy 1.1 places the record in the notes of the response and in the report to court.
The federal bar on apprehension for socio-economic conditions applies 'to the extent that it is consistent with the best interests of the child'. The provincial rule applies to two of the grounds for protection. The requirement records a finding and leaves the judgement to the decision-maker.
The federal Act Q&A (practice only) says addiction or mental health concerns alone are not grounds to remove a child. That reading of 'state of health' has no legislation or policy behind it in the documents held (R-IN4-13).
The federal Act's exception is where 'immediate apprehension is consistent with the best interests of the child'. Policy 1.1 states the exception as the child's health or safety being in immediate danger.

Rationale
The federal Act requires the service provider to demonstrate, before apprehending an Indigenous child who lives with a parent or adult family member, that reasonable efforts were made to have the child stay with that person (s. 15.1), and gives priority to preventive care (s. 14). Rationale
The Act lets the court attach terms the director recommends, including a term that requires removal on breach, and then requires removal without a further order when such a term is breached or the order no longer protects the child (CFCSA ss. 36(1), 41.1, 42(1)). Policy bars recommending that term for an Indigenous child. LEG001-C53

The content of a plan of care is required in full by P12. This requirement covers only its use in a court application.

Chapter 4 lists three terms to recommend (cooperation, visits and inspection, removal on non-compliance). Chapter 3 lists two and omits visits and inspection. Both are current policy; the list is data.
The criteria for the permanent transfers of custody (Procedure 2(d) to (f)) and the consents they need are specified in pack P11.
The provincial and territorial protocol on children moving between provinces is not held.
Rationale
Chapter 4 requires the worker to determine that an out-of-care arrangement is the best plan against criteria that differ by kind of arrangement, to plan with the child's circle, and to document the child's needs, the child's views and the results of planning. Chapters 3 and 4 both list terms to recommend to the court for an order under the director's supervision. CFD294-C2

FR-204 Must M9 High
Approving and implementing a permanency plan, and the legal steps its time limits require

Given a permanency plan with no supervisor's approval recorded, when a worker marks it as being implemented, then the system refuses and routes the plan to a supervisor.

The Act counts its limit from the date of the initial temporary custody order, by the age of the youngest child in that order (CK-LG1-31). Policy 6.2(3) counts from the child leaving the parents' care, by the child's own age (CK-AD1-43). They are two clocks with different start events; the system runs both and the Act's is the legal limit.

Chapter 4 says 'age 12 or older' at L182 and L417 and 'over age 12' at L303, L328 and L360; Policy 6.3 also says 'over age 12'. The Act prevails and the age is data, so the requirement is unchanged. The policy wording needs correcting (ministry question).
For a transfer after a temporary custody order the Act does not require the parents' consent (s. 54.01(5)(b)(ii)); Chapter 4 lists the parent as one who 'may' sign. The system lists it as optional.
Policy says independent legal advice 'should be offered'; the Act says the court must be satisfied the person 'has been advised to consult'. The system records the offer and does not require that advice was taken.
No source states how a consent to a permanent transfer is withdrawn before the order is made.
Rationale
The Act lets a court transfer custody permanently only where named persons have consented, and lets it rely on a consent only if the person was advised to consult independent legal counsel, understands the consent and gave it voluntarily. Policy requires the Public Guardian and Trustee's consent before the application. LEG001-C58
FR-209 Must M0 Medium
Guardianship under a custody order to another person, and the effects of a permanent transfer
The system records who holds guardianship rights and responsibilities for a child under an interim or temporary custody order to a person other than a parent, including any right the court leaves with the parent. Show detail
First needed in: M0 (schema), M9
Description
The system records who holds guardianship rights and responsibilities for a child under an interim or temporary custody order to a person other than a parent, including any right the court leaves with the parent. When a permanent transfer of custody order is made, it records the person as the child's guardian, ends the director's custody, treats the order as one that cannot be enforced, modified or cancelled under the Act, and changes the standing of existing access orders. FR-212 Must M9 Medium

Description
The system runs the cycle of a child's care plan. The Infants Act is not in this pack's sources. The Act's own words on the child's right were read (CFCSA s. 47(4); Adoption Act s. 27(4)). Pack P49 holds the Infants Act rows.
Who may consent for a child in care under a voluntary care or special needs agreement is set by the agreement (pack P08a). The medical record form lists it as a source of authority (practice only).
The medical record form still lists the repealed Family Relations Act as a source of authority (R-GU1-36, not current). The system should not offer it.
