N12
NFR-SEC-013 Must
Access follows the service line and the Act that governs the record
Access rules for children and family services are written per service line and tested as code (NFR-SEC-002). Show detail
Priority: MUST_HAVE (M0 schema, M9) ---
Requirement
Access rules for children and family services are written per service line and tested as code (NFR-SEC-002). A support needs worker delivering a service outside the CFCSA mandate cannot open child protection or other CFCSA records. A child protection worker cannot open a family's support needs record. Information passes between the two only on a recorded basis: consent, or a request under the Act. The Act that governs each record is recorded on it and decides who may see it. Psychological test data is open only to qualified test users. Within an integrated team, a declined consent to share limits reading to the serving member and the people policy names, and a clinical note is never readable through the shared view. During a pending transfer the receiving office has read access, so access follows the state of the transfer and not office membership alone. Every director and delegate, delegated agencies included, can read every community agreement.
Measurement Method
An automated test for each pair of service lines attempts to open the other's records and is refused, and each refused attempt appears in the access log (NFR-SEC-004). The test set is run on every release.
Rationale
Policy bars access across the support needs and child protection lines in both directions and sets the other limits (CL-D6-026, CL-D6-027, CL-D6-028, CL-D1-106, R-RX1-06, CL-D5-157, CL-D5-158, R-IC1-15, CL-D5-109, CL-D7-008, R-MH2-42). An access rule that does not exist before the first record is written leaves earlier records open. Needed by FR-117, FR-118, FR-289, FR-291, FR-377, FR-389, FR-395 and FR-398. The access rule for mental health clinical records is described only in a user manual, so the ministry should state it as policy first (R-MH1-41, AU-MH1-20). The mental health and integrated team parts are conditional on DEP-26 and DEP-27.
Parameters
N21, N13, N18
NFR-SEC-014 Must
An access bar on a person holds against every role that person has
Where a staff member is also the subject of a record, the bar follows the person and not the role. Show detail
Priority: MUST_HAVE ---
Requirement
Where a staff member is also the subject of a record, the bar follows the person and not the role. An employee who is a foster caregiver cannot open records relating to the children they foster, whatever role they hold, and decisions on their own foster care arrangement go to a director of operations outside their chain of command. An employee does not serve, as an employee, a person recorded as one they have seen in private counselling work. A report of a search, a refusal or a detention of a staff member cannot be read by that person's peers or from a youth's file. People with permission to see information but no authority to act, such as those in a practicum category of delegation, can read and cannot record a director's act. Staff who review records for a prior contact check, an audit or a foster caregiver review are given access limited to the person or the evaluation named, and each access records that purpose.
Measurement Method
Tests give one person two roles and show that the bar holds in each. Refused attempts are logged and reviewed (NFR-SEC-004). A sample of review and audit accesses is checked against the consent or the evaluation scope on record.
Rationale
The ministry's guidance requires these safeguards where it permits an employee to foster or to do private counselling work, and policy scopes access for checks and audits (OB-RF1-40, OB-QA1-22, CL-D2-009, RC-GU1-06, CL-D1-006, CL-D3-169, CL-D3-170, CL-D3-171, CL-D3-172). Needed by FR-107, FR-226, FR-229, FR-345, FR-347 and FR-472. The custody search records are conditional on DEP-28. Practice guidance also restricts staff members' own homestudies further (R-AD4-13), which is to confirm against current policy.
Parameters
N17, N18, N21
NFR-SEC-015 Must
What a person may learn about the existence of a record is itself an access rule
The system sets, for each record class, whether a person without access to the content may learn that a record exists. Show detail
Priority: MUST_HAVE ---
Requirement
The system sets, for each record class, whether a person without access to the content may learn that a record exists. A person search by a support needs worker shows that a record exists without opening it. A safety alert and its recommended actions are shown to all staff who meet the child, youth or family, including staff who cannot see the clinical record behind it. A safety plan agreement, its copies and its notices are visible only to the parties to that agreement, so that an agreement made with one parent alone need not be made known to the other where domestic violence is a factor. Any record class can be restricted, contact and identity records included, and a restricted record is open only to the limited group policy names.
Measurement Method
For each record class a test signs in as a person without content access and compares what the search, the alert view and the notice list show against the rule registered for that class.
Rationale
Policy sets each of these visibility rules (CL-D6-027, CL-D6-028, OB-MH2-15, CL-D5-007, CL-D1-062, CL-D8-001, CL-D8-006). Needed by FR-164, FR-291, FR-299 and FR-351. The alert rule is conditional on DEP-26.

Domain events
Evidence, determination, case, payment, overpayment, appeal and identity events
Full transitive compatibility: backward and forward compatible against every prior version
Reference-data events
Rate tables, program codes, value lists, reason codes
Backward compatibility, plus a stability contract: a published code is never reused for a different meaning, and retirement is a state transition, not a deletion
Integration and telemetry events
Anti-corruption layer signals, observability, the platform capabilities' events
Backward compatibility, no replay guarantee; no projection may be built on them
Coded values. A coded-value field in an event schema is either a string validated at the edge against its reference-data master, or an enumeration with a mandatory default symbol (UNKNOWN) to which unrecognised values resolve. A schema registering a closed enumeration without a default is rejected at publish. The closed-enumeration rule binds API contracts and command validation, not event wire schemas. A consumer that resolves a value to UNKNOWN preserves the raw value and routes the record to its exception path where the field is material.
Upcasters are complementary, not an alternative: every upcaster is a versioned artefact exercised by a replay test against archived events in the owning context's pipeline.
Measurement Method
The registry rejects a domain-event schema that is not fully transitively compatible, and a closed enumeration without a default. A replay test from origin runs in each owning context's pipeline.
Rationale
Breaking replay of an old event is a data-loss incident (TA §B.5.4, §D.1). A "backward compatible" change that breaks replay of a five-year-old event is exactly that, which is why domain events carry the stricter class.
Parameters
N10, N18, N01
NFR-I-004 Must
Delivery rules and safe retries
Events are delivered at least once through a transactional outbox. Show detail
Priority: MUST_HAVE ---
Requirement
Events are delivered at least once through a transactional outbox. Every consumer is idempotent, so a repeated message has no extra effect. Ordering guarantees are stated for each stream.
Amended 2026-09-30 (drift B10; TA §B.5.2, §B.5.3): every consumer of a domain event meets this contract, checked at release:
The partition key is aggregate_id. The broker orders only within a partition, so per-aggregate ordering needs per-aggregate partitioning. Repartitioning is a breaking change, governed like a schema break: announced, versioned, with a migration path and a sunset period.
event_id governs deduplication; aggregate_version governs ordering. Apply is idempotent on event_id, through a naturally idempotent write or a processed-id store whose time-to-live is no shorter than the maximum replay window.
aggregate_version is used for gap detection and bounded buffering, never for rejection. A consumer that sees a version higher than expected buffers up to a bound and waits for the gap to fill. On timeout it escalates to a named recovery path (replay from offset, or a monitored reconciliation queue with a named owner), never to a dead-letter queue.
Replay epoch. A replay from origin is published under an incremented replay_epoch. A consumer that sees a new epoch rebuilds its projection from empty instead of applying incrementally.
The relay reads the outbox in commit order (log-based capture, or a sequence assigned at commit). A polling relay over an identity column is not acceptable where events affect entitlement, payment or debt.
Measurement Method
Conformance tests at release: duplicate, reordered and gapped deliveries per aggregate; a full replay under a new epoch; concurrent-commit tests of the relay.
Rationale
At-least-once delivery on a payment path is safe only if idempotency is designed in (TA §C.6.8). Rejecting an out-of-order event discards data the broker will not re-deliver and turns a normal reordering into permanent divergence (TA §B.5.2).
Parameters
N06, N05, N18
NFR-I-005 Must
Ministry-owned formats and portable records
Decision records, evidence and documents are held in formats the ministry owns. Show detail
Priority: MUST_HAVE ---
Requirement
Decision records, evidence and documents are held in formats the ministry owns. The ministry can export them without a vendor's tools, including a transfer package with its offline verifier.
Export Formats
Open, documented formats for each record class, with published schemas.
Rationale
Replay must still work after every component that produced the decision has been retired (PRIN N08).
Parameters
N08, N13
NFR-I-006 Must
Open standards, and buying what is generic
The system uses open standards throughout, and prefers open source for generic needs. Show detail
Priority: MUST_HAVE ---
Requirement
The system uses open standards throughout, and prefers open source for generic needs. It buys, adopts or reuses workflow, notification, identity, secrets, policy evaluation, scheduling, document storage, search and print-and-mail. Any decision to build one of these must name the statutory, policy or program requirement that no commodity option meets. Someone other than the component's owner assesses the claim TA-C41. Each selection records the open alternative that was rejected.
Before procurement, custom build is evaluated against commercial and reusable case management platforms for the platform as a whole, and that evaluation is assessed independently.
Rationale
The platform-level build-or-buy question is the largest open question in the architecture, and leaving it open breaks the architecture's own rules PRIN-C9.
Parameters
N11
NFR-I-007 Should
API styles
REST for commands, resources and bulk operations. Show detail
Priority: SHOULD_HAVE ---
Requirement
REST for commands, resources and bulk operations. GraphQL for combined reads during transactions, with persisted operations mandatory. Access control, audit, versioning and idempotency are applied the same way at the Open Host Service.
Rationale
This is the recommendation of decision D2. Shared caching is not possible for responses about individual people (TA §C.1.4).
Parameters
N10, N02
NFR-I-008 Must
Five program-family case contexts that share protocols, not a case model
Added 2026-09-30 (drift B8; Show detail
Priority: MUST_HAVE ---
Description
Added 2026-09-30 (drift B8; ADR-001).
Requirement
Case delivery is five domain contexts, one per program family: Case: employment assistance · Case: persons with disabilities · Case: child care subsidy · Case: employment services · Case: child protection. Each has its own persistence, topics, published language, lifecycle and owning team. They share protocols, not a case model: each consumes identity events, records evidence through Evidence & Verification, requests determinations from Eligibility & Entitlement (Determination), requests services, instructs Financial Components, raises work in Work Management, and emits correspondence triggers to Notices & Correspondence. No type, table or lifecycle is shared between them. "Case & Service Delivery" names the family only; it is never the owner of a requirement, obligation, aggregate or event. The owner is always one case context, or "all case contexts (shared protocol)" where an obligation is common to all five.
Measurement Method
Dependency analysis in CI shows no case context depending on another's types or store. The traceability file names a specific case context, or the shared protocol, on every case-delivery row. Each case context can be released on its own.
Rationale
A child protection investigation and a child care subsidy renewal share no meaningful state model. A shared case model is the meta-model the predecessor programme could not change; some duplicated case plumbing is far cheaper (TA §B.2.1). Employment assistance and persons-with-disabilities assistance are governed by one policy manual, but they are still two contexts.
Relates To
NFR-I-002, FR-032, FR-067
Parameters
N03, N05
DRAFT
A design proposal for the successor to British Columbia's integrated case management systems, covering employment assistance, disability assistance, child care subsidy, employment services and child protection.
Figures on this site are drawn from the architecture document, from 326 service-delivery procedures, and from 308 documents and 14 statutes and regulations on children and family services. Nothing here is a government commitment.

Trade-offs and open decisions
Some requirements pull against each other. These conflicts come from the sources themselves: policy against practice, one design parameter against another, a legal duty against a design property. Each one says what was chosen, what it costs, and who decides.
[aria-label] Conflict status
13 conflicts set out
7 resolved by the source hierarchy or the architecture
6 waiting on a ministry ruling
C-1 PRIORITIZE (policy), with INNOVATE (Option 3) Resolved
Policy against practice on the right to challenge
Decision: Option 3. Every request is recorded, and the pre-decision communication tells clients truthfully where they stand. Who decides: The source hierarchy settles the requirement. The ministry (ADM Policy and Program Design) is asked to correct the procedures (DEP-10).
Conflicting Requirements:
Requirement A: FR-055. A reconsideration request is always accepted and recorded, and the independent unit decides whether reconsideration is available (FR-056).
Requirement B: Current procedures. Staff are told "Do not offer the right to reconsideration" when food vouchers are denied RECON-C1; overpayment workers are told to answer a request with "there is nothing to reconsider"; and the brochure is held back when an overpayment is notified (RC-01, RC-14).
Stakeholders Involved:
Reconsideration and Administrative Fairness Unit and the policy authority: policy gives an unconditional right to ask.
Front-line service delivery: procedures were written to stop early or pointless requests and keep queues manageable.
Nature of Conflict:
A request cannot both be refused at the counter and recorded. In practice, the worker decides whether reconsideration is available, which they have no authority to do.
Trade-off Analysis:
Option
Pros
Cons
Impact
Option 1: Follow policy. Record every request and decide availability centrally
✅ Lawful<br>✅ Consistent across channels
❌ More requests reach the independent unit
Policy authority satisfied; the unit's workload rises
Option 2: Follow practice. Allow refusal at the point of contact
✅ Fewer requests
❌ Contradicts policy, which takes precedence<br>❌ Refusals nobody can review
Rejected by the source hierarchy
Option 3: Record every request, and use the pre-decision communication to tell clients that no decision has been made yet (FR-006)
✅ Lawful<br>✅ Fewer pointless requests, because clients know where they stand
❌ Needs the proposal object
Meets each side's underlying interest
Resolution Strategy: PRIORITIZE (policy), with INNOVATE (Option 3)
Decision: Option 3. Every request is recorded, and the pre-decision communication tells clients truthfully where they stand.
Rationale: Policy takes precedence over practice (BC-1). The ministry's own intake practice already uses the pre-decision pattern correctly (NOTE-001).
Decision Authority: The source hierarchy settles the requirement. The ministry (ADM Policy and Program Design) is asked to correct the procedures (DEP-10).
Impact on Requirements:
Added: FR-006 (pre-decision communication), FR-056 (availability decided by the independent unit).
Recorded: RC-01 and RC-14 as practice defects for the ministry to correct.
Stakeholder Management:
Front-line service delivery (bears the cost): the pre-decision communication gives workers a correct, scripted route. The independent unit's request volume is monitored.
Future Consideration:
After M7, measure request volume by channel and adjust staffing, not the right.
C-2 COMPROMISE Resolved
A history that is never changed against the duty to destroy records
Decision: Option 3 (TA §B.7; decision D13). Who decides: Ministry Records Officer with the Privacy Officer and the Chief Architect (D13), before the first production event.
Conflicting Requirements:
Requirement A: FR-008, DR-001. A permanent history that can be replayed, with nothing overwritten.
Requirement B: NFR-C-003, DR-004. Records destroyed on schedule, and one person's records destroyed where a duty or order requires it.
Stakeholders Involved:
Chief Architect: a tribunal examines whether decisions can be reproduced.
Records Officer and Privacy Officer: destroying records on schedule is a legal duty.
Nature of Conflict:
A store that never forgets cannot destroy anything, and a store that destroys records cannot replay everything.
Trade-off Analysis:
Option
Pros
Cons
Impact
Option 1: Encrypt everything per person and destroy keys
✅ Any one person's records can be destroyed
❌ The most expensive method for every fact<br>❌ The conflict between backing up keys and destroying them applies everywhere
Over-built
Option 2: Never destroy anything in the event store
✅ Full replay forever
❌ Breaks the records duty
Rejected
Option 3: A disposal method per fact class, a published shred-survivor list, typed placeholders for destroyed facts, and an advance statement of what can no longer be reproduced
✅ Meets each duty where it applies<br>✅ Cost in proportion
❌ Replay is limited for people whose records were destroyed, and this must be said in advance
Both duties met, with a stated limit
Resolution Strategy: COMPROMISE
Decision: Option 3 (TA §B.7; decision D13).
Rationale: The common duty is scheduled disposal of a whole class of records, not erasure on request. Designing the whole store around the rare case buys the wrong capability.
Decision Authority: Ministry Records Officer with the Privacy Officer and the Chief Architect (D13), before the first production event.
Impact on Requirements:
Modified: FR-008 carries the declared limit on replay; DR-004 requires the survivor list before the first event.
Stakeholder Management:
Chief Architect (loses unlimited replay): the limit is declared before the first disposal, not discovered at the first challenge.
Future Consideration:
Revisit the method for each fact class once the ARCS/ORCS schedules are obtained (DEP-09).
C-3 INNOVATE Open
Reaching every client against a verification check tied to how they are paid
Decision: Option 3, subject to a ministry ruling (DEP-10). Until then, clients can choose office pickup as a payment channel, but it is never used as the check. Who decides: ADM Policy and Program Design.
Conflicting Requirements:
Requirement A: FR-086, BR-009. Outcomes do not depend on channel, and electronic payment is available.
Requirement B: OB-SU-61. Hardship cheques are sent to the local office so that eligibility is re-checked every month.
Stakeholders Involved:
Head of Service Delivery Operations and clients: reach and dignity; clients should not have to visit an office every month to get paid.
Policy authority and compliance: hardship eligibility re-checked every month.
Nature of Conflict:
One mechanism meets two requirements. Paying electronically removes the monthly check PRIN-C8.
Trade-off Analysis:
Option
Pros
Cons
Impact
Option 1: Keep sending cheques to the office
✅ Check preserved
❌ Clients must travel to an office to be paid
Clients bear the cost
Option 2: Pay electronically and drop the check
✅ Better reach
❌ Removes a policy control
Compliance bears the risk
Option 3: Separate the two. A monthly re-check work item that applies whatever the channel (FR-040), with the client choosing how to be paid
✅ Both requirements met
❌ Needs a policy ruling on what counts as a re-check
Both met if policy agrees
Resolution Strategy: INNOVATE
Decision: Option 3, subject to a ministry ruling (DEP-10). Until then, clients can choose office pickup as a payment channel, but it is never used as the check.
Rationale: N15 has exposed two requirements met by one mechanism, which nobody saw until it was written down (PRIN N15).
Decision Authority: ADM Policy and Program Design.
Impact on Requirements:
Modified: FR-040 makes the monthly re-check a work item whatever the channel.
Stakeholder Management:
Compliance (loses the incidental check): a stated re-check that can be audited replaces an unstated one.
Future Consideration:
The same pattern may exist elsewhere. Phase D should look for controls that depend on a channel.
C-4 INNOVATE Resolved
Changing policy quickly against releasing rules that will stand up at tribunal
Decision: Option 3 (commitment 2; TA §C.4.3). Who decides: The Chief Architect and the ADM Policy and Program Design, jointly, as the authority that can relax commitment 2.
Conflicting Requirements:
Requirement A: BR-010. Policy staff release rate changes on their effective date without a software release.
Requirement B: FR-090, FR-091, FR-003. Release needs a second person's approval, legal sign-off, a regression test set, approval of decision classes, and no unresolved date conflicts.
Stakeholders Involved:
ADM Policy and Program Design: changes take effect on the date the minister sets.
Chief Architect and legal counsel: every release must stand up at tribunal.
Nature of Conflict:
Every check slows release. Removing checks makes releases harder to defend.
Trade-off Analysis:
Option
Pros
Cons
Impact
Option 1: Rules written in code and released with software
✅ Engineering controls
❌ Every rate change waits for a software release
Policy frustrated
Option 2: Analysts release rules freely
✅ Speed
❌ Releases that cannot be defended
Legal exposure
Option 3: An automated release pipeline. Simulation, regression and classification checks run automatically; people only review and give legal sign-off, and do so before the effective date
✅ Speed and defensibility
❌ The pipeline must be funded as a product
Both met
Resolution Strategy: INNOVATE
Decision: Option 3 (commitment 2; TA §C.4.3).
Rationale: Release and effect are separate. A rule released early takes effect on its stated date.
Decision Authority: The Chief Architect and the ADM Policy and Program Design, jointly, as the authority that can relax commitment 2.
Impact on Requirements:
Added: FR-091 blocks rules with date conflicts; DEP-14 tests analyst capability.
Stakeholder Management:
Policy (loses the ability to release alone): policy staff run the pipeline themselves, and the capability test proves they can before D3 is final.
Future Consideration:
If DEP-14 fails, improve the authoring tools rather than remove the checks.
C-5 COMPROMISE Resolved
Automated decisions at scale against the need for a human decision-maker
Decision: Option 3. Who decides: The statutory decision-maker for each program authorises each class (FR-093). The program policy authority approves the classification on legal advice.
Conflicting Requirements:
Requirement A: NFR-P-003, BR-004. Decisions and payments for the whole caseload, on time.
Requirement B: FR-003, FR-052, NFR-C-005. A human must decide any adverse decision based on inferred data, and every overpayment.
Stakeholders Involved:
Service delivery operations: volume and timeliness.
Statutory decision-makers and legal counsel: lawful administrative decisions.
Nature of Conflict:
Human review of every decision cannot keep up with the volume. Elsewhere, decisions with no human review have produced unlawful debt at scale.
Trade-off Analysis:
Option
Pros
Cons
Impact
Option 1: A person reviews every decision
✅ Safe
❌ Unworkable volume; late decisions change what clients are owed (FR-061)
Clients harmed by delay
Option 2: Automate everything
✅ Fast
❌ Unlawful for discretionary decisions and adverse decisions based on inference
Rejected
Option 3: Classify each output. Automate only verified administrative decisions with no discretion, under the four conditions in TA §D.5.2. A person decides anything involving discretion or inference, and every overpayment. A class is suspended automatically if challenges succeed too often
✅ Automates where lawful<br>✅ Safe where not
❌ Classification has to be governed
Both met, class by class
Resolution Strategy: COMPROMISE
Decision: Option 3.
Rationale: What the comparator jurisdiction lacked was a rule about which outputs count as decisions (TA §D.5).
Decision Authority: The statutory decision-maker for each program authorises each class (FR-093). The program policy authority approves the classification on legal advice.
Impact on Requirements:
Added: FR-093 register and suspension triggers.
Stakeholder Management:
Service delivery (loses full automation): volume by class is published every cycle, so the line between automated and human decisions is argued from evidence.
Future Consideration:
Review each class every year, and whenever challenges pass their trigger.
C-6 PHASE Open
Paying on time against verifying first
Decision: Option 3, pending a ministry ruling on which checks may be done after payment (DEP-10). Who decides: Program policy authority.
Conflicting Requirements:
Requirement A: NFR-A-008. No client's payment waits on another organisation's gateway. Decisions go ahead on the evidence held and are flagged for later checking.
Requirement B: FR-015. Mandatory third-party checks at application and review, unless a registered deferral applies.
Stakeholders Involved:
Clients and service delivery: payment on the due date.
Compliance and the policy authority: eligibility checked before assistance is paid.
Nature of Conflict:
When the exchange is down, the system must either pay without a mandatory check or hold the payment.
Trade-off Analysis:
Option
Pros
Cons
Impact
Option 1: Hold every decision until checks complete
✅ Checks preserved
❌ Payment depends on an outside gateway
Clients bear the outages
Option 2: Always go ahead and check later
✅ Payment on time
❌ Breaks the mandatory-check policy where no deferral applies
Compliance risk
Option 3: Go ahead only where a registered deferral applies or policy allows checking after payment; otherwise use emergency issuance under authority (FR-047) and reconcile later
✅ Lawful and on time
❌ Needs policy to state the deferral cases
Both met within policy
Resolution Strategy: PHASE
Decision: Option 3, pending a ministry ruling on which checks may be done after payment (DEP-10).
Rationale: For this failure, the architecture names the program policy authority as the one who decides whether to go ahead on the evidence held (TA §E.8.3).
Decision Authority: Program policy authority.
Impact on Requirements:
Modified: NFR-A-008 applies only to cases policy allows.
Stakeholder Management:
Compliance: every check done after payment is a tracked work item with its own deadline.
Future Consideration:
Revisit once the exchange commits to an availability target (DEP-06).
C-7 COMPROMISE Resolved
Keeping old reports and interfaces working against the detail the new record holds
Decision: Option 3 (TA §C.2.6; DR-014, DR-015). Who decides: The Policy Directors accept the published losses for each part of the system and each group of clients; the Coexistence Lead owns the mechanism.
Conflicting Requirements:
Requirement A: DR-014. Write changes back to the old system for groups of clients the new system has taken over, so old reports, batch jobs and interfaces not yet moved keep working.
Requirement B: DR-001, DR-002. The new record holds dates, lifecycle and source detail the old system's structure cannot hold.
Stakeholders Involved:
Users of the old systems and operations staff: things keep working while both systems run.
Program policy authority: accountable for what a rollback loses.
Nature of Conflict:
Writing back always loses detail, so every day in state S2 is a day on an incomplete copy.
Trade-off Analysis:
Option
Pros
Cons
Impact
Option 1: No write-back; move every user of the old data in one cutover
✅ No loss
❌ The single-cutover risk the evidence from other jurisdictions rules out
Rejected
Option 2: Write back indefinitely
✅ Old systems keep working
❌ Running both systems becomes permanent
How the predecessor programme failed
Option 3: Write back for a limited time and with limited detail. The losses are published and accepted per fact class, and a retirement date is set when each group moves
✅ Old systems keep working, at a stated cost and with an end date
❌ Named losses must be accepted
Both met, with a stated limit
Resolution Strategy: COMPROMISE
Decision: Option 3 (TA §C.2.6; DR-014, DR-015).
Rationale: Claiming a move can be reversed without saying what is lost means the cost has not been worked out.
Decision Authority: The Policy Directors accept the published losses for each part of the system and each group of clients; the Coexistence Lead owns the mechanism.
Impact on Requirements:
Added: DR-015's published list of losses, including the difference between a correction and a supersession.
Stakeholder Management:
Program policy authority (accepts named losses): acceptance is explicit, for each group of clients, before state S2.
Future Consideration:
Retire each user of the old data as parts of the system reach state S3.
C-8 PHASE Resolved
Building the ministry-specific parts against buying a platform
Decision: Option 3 (DEP-19). This document does not assume a particular solution, so it can serve as the baseline for that evaluation (A-7). Who decides: ED Digital Services with the ADM Policy and Program Design (D3), assessed by someone other than the owners of the parts.
Conflicting Requirements:
Requirement A: NFR-I-006. Buy generic capability, have any decision to build assessed independently, and evaluate the whole platform against commercial and reusable case management platforms.
Requirement B: The architecture's list of parts to build (the evidence store, the decision machinery, case handling, the translation layer, the exchange's authorization and evidence services, overpayment, appeals, and identity matching) (TA §C.18.1).
Stakeholders Involved:

Chief Architect: owns the reasons for each part to be built.
Nature of Conflict:
The architecture has not applied its own build-or-buy test to the platform as a whole, and three of its eight build decisions fail that test (PRIN N11).
Trade-off Analysis:
Option
Pros
Cons
Impact

✅ Keeps the architecture as it is
❌ Fails the architecture's own rule

C-9 PHASE Open
Two statutes set different placement priorities for an Indigenous child
Decision: Option 1, pending a legal ruling on which statute governs (MQ-023). Who decides: Legal counsel to the ministry, with the Indigenous Child Welfare Director.
Conflicting Requirements:
Requirement A: the placement priority in section 16(1) of the federal Act, which places a parent first and separates family from community.
Requirement B: the placement priority in section 71(3) of the CFCSA, which does neither. The adoption policy and the care plan form follow it; Policy 1.1 follows the federal order.
Stakeholders Involved:
Indigenous governing bodies and communities: the federal Act sets minimum standards for their children.
Directors and delegated workers: must record which order was applied to each placement.
Nature of Conflict:
The two orders can give different answers for the same child. Which governs, and whether the federal order reaches adoption matching, is a legal question the source hierarchy does not answer.
Trade-off Analysis:
Option
Pros
Cons
Impact
Option 1: Hold both orders as rule data and record which was applied, with the reasons
✅ Builds now<br>✅ No change when the question is answered
❌ The system cannot say a placement is out of order
Decision stays with the director
Option 2: Build one order
✅ The system can test a placement
❌ May be the wrong order in law
Rejected until counsel rules
Resolution Strategy: PHASE
Decision: Option 1, pending a legal ruling on which statute governs (MQ-023).
Rationale: A rule held as data can be changed on its effective date (BR-010). A rule built into the system cannot.
Decision Authority: Legal counsel to the ministry, with the Indigenous Child Welfare Director.
Impact on Requirements:
Recorded: the placement priority requirement in group CF2 holds both orders and the reasons for each placement.
Stakeholder Management:
Indigenous governing bodies: the notice of a significant measure tells them of the placement decided.
Future Consideration:
When the ruling is made, release the governing order as a dated rule.
C-10 PRIORITIZE (the statutes) Resolved
One view of a child against records each service line must keep apart
Decision: Option 2. The statutes prevail over convenience. Who decides: The source hierarchy settles the requirement. The Ministry Privacy Officer rules on any class of record not covered.
Conflicting Requirements:
Requirement A: BR-012 and FR-032. A worker sees the history they need, and a supervisor sees caseloads across programs.
Requirement B: BR-022 and the requirements in groups CF10, CF12, CF15 and CF18. Support needs staff and child protection staff do not open each other's records without consent or a written request. Youth justice information is kept out of the mental health record. A restricted record is seen only by a named group.
Stakeholders Involved:
Workers and supervisors: need the full picture to keep a child safe.
Children, youth and families: the statutes limit who may see what was collected for one purpose.
Nature of Conflict:
A shared person index and a composite view show that a record exists. In these services the existence of a record is often the sensitive fact.
Trade-off Analysis:
Option
Pros
Cons
Impact
Option 1: One view, filtered by role
✅ Simple for workers
❌ A filter that fails shows everything
Rejected: a restricted record is a different type, not a hidden field (TA §B.6)
Option 2: Limits on use travel with each record class, and the index answers only what the asker may know (N21)
✅ Lawful<br>✅ The limit survives every copy
❌ A worker may not learn that another line knows the child
Each line keeps its own record; sharing goes through a recorded consent or request
Resolution Strategy: PRIORITIZE (the statutes)
Decision: Option 2. The statutes prevail over convenience.
Rationale: Legislation comes first (BC-7). FR-080 already requires a barred use to be blocked at the point of use.
Decision Authority: The source hierarchy settles the requirement. The Ministry Privacy Officer rules on any class of record not covered.
Impact on Requirements:
Added: criteria on FR-084 for a record class a federal statute governs.
Open: what happens to a restriction when a record transfers or is jointly managed is stated in no source.
Stakeholder Management:
Workers (bear the cost): the duty to report a child in need of protection is unaffected, and a written request under the Act remains the route to another line's record.
Future Consideration:
Measure, in discovery for M9, how often a worker needed a record they could not see.
C-11 PHASE Open
A store that never overwrites against provisions that require removal
Decision: Option 1 is preferred, subject to decision D13 on how each fact class is destroyed (DEP-07). Who decides: Ministry Records Officer with the Privacy Officer.
Conflicting Requirements:
Requirement A: BR-007 and DR-004. History is permanent, and disposal is designed before the first record.
Requirement B: adoption and privacy provisions that require information to be removed: registry information when a registration ends, the proposal package from an applicant's record on decline or disruption, and misdirected information that the privacy statute treats as not collected only if it is deleted or returned.
Stakeholders Involved:
Ministry Records Officer and Privacy Officer: own disposal.
Adoptive applicants, birth parents and adopted people: the Act protects their information.
Nature of Conflict:
These are removals on an event in one person's matter, not disposal of a class of records on a schedule. C-2 settled the second and did not consider the first.
Trade-off Analysis:
Option
Pros
Cons
Impact
Option 1: Treat each removal as a disposal event under DR-004, with a record that the removal happened
✅ One mechanism
❌ Needs per-record disposal, not only per-class
Extends decision D13
Option 2: Hold these classes outside the permanent store
✅ Simple removal
❌ A second store with its own controls
Against N05
Resolution Strategy: PHASE
Decision: Option 1 is preferred, subject to decision D13 on how each fact class is destroyed (DEP-07).
Rationale: The removal is a legal duty; the fact that it happened is itself a record the ministry must be able to show.
Decision Authority: Ministry Records Officer with the Privacy Officer.
Impact on Requirements:
Added: a criterion on DR-004 for the minimum retention the privacy statute sets.
Open: per-record removal is not yet a requirement.
Stakeholder Management:
Records Officer: the classes concerned are listed in the data requirements for children's services.
Future Consideration:
Settle with D13, before the first production event.
C-12 PHASE Open

Conflicting Requirements:

Requirement B: ministry finance policy. Immediate office payments for children's services are drawn on a bank account managed by another ministry, on its own cheque stock, with cheques printed in the office.

A second route to the bank is a second set of controls, audited separately (TA §C.6.8).

A PWD* designation granted in July.
A boundary that lives only in a diagram will not survive delivery pressure. These six are written so a reviewer can point at something and say whether it complies.
A client can still ask for a reconsideration at that point. The request is always recorded, and nobody turns it away at the counter. Whether a reconsideration is available is decided by the independent reconsideration unit, not by the worker who sent the letter.
A client waiting for a reconsideration or an appeal may keep receiving assistance at the old level. That money is paid on a promise to repay whatever the final decision does not support. The system holds it as repayable from the day it is paid, linked to the decision it is waiting for, and settles it automatically when that decision is made.
A conventional design holds one relationship start date, plus an audit entry saying a worker changed it on 12 September. That answers the third question, gestures at the second, and cannot touch the first. It leaves the eight monthly payments looking like errors. Each one was the right answer to what the ministry knew at the time.
A database table
A decision records the moment its facts were read
A decision that is overturned is never edited. The original stays in the record as what was decided, with everything it was based on. The new decision sits beside it, with its own record, and says what caused it. The client's history shows both, in order, with reasons. The money owed either way is worked out from the difference between the two.
A decision you can re-run
A design proposal for the successor to British Columbia's integrated case management systems, covering employment assistance, disability assistance, child care subsidy, employment services and child protection.
A design proposal for the successor to British Columbia's integrated case management systems, explained in plain English.
A document is not evidence.
A document is what a verification policy accepts as satisfying an evidence type. Losing that distinction turns the file store into a second system of record.
A fact carries a note of where it came from. A database row doesn’t. The part that receives a bare row can’t tell who said it, so it can’t know what it is safe to conclude. And if the source later fixes the value, there is nothing to attach the fix to.
A first assertion about a period nothing covered yet.
A limit missing when information is first collected is missing from every copy made before it was added
A link to a system that is still running is not proof. You have to be able to replay a decision long after the systems that made it are gone, the rules engine included. The client also has a right to the record itself, gathered together, with protected details removed as FOIPPA requires. Being able to replay a decision doesn’t give them that.
A modernisation has to know what it is replacing. The rules that decide entitlement sit in six separate places. Only one of them is a rules engine, and the one that carries authority, the policy manual, can only be read by a person.
A parameter is something a system must comply with. A parameter must be check-able; it must be possible to check whether the system complies to it. To make sure that these rules are parameters, every entry below ends in a question you can put to a running system and get a wrong answer to.
A part that needs another's data keeps its own copy, built from that part's events and shaped the way it needs. When the source corrects something, the copy has to follow.
A partner moves in on 1 May, and the client reports it.
A person can get the same result whatever their disability and whichever way they contact the ministry. Screens and forms meet the Province’s accessibility standard from the first release. And every service has a supported way to use it that isn’t online.
A pointer resolves to whatever the database says today. Replay returns today’s answer to a four-year-old question.
A published interface for reads, and published events for notices. There is no third way, and adding one is not a shortcut.
A review establishes the household was a couple from January, not a single person.
A rule nobody can check is not a rule
A rules engine
A store built without a plan for destroying records can’t get one later
A system that stores only the current state, "Income: $900", leaves the important questions open. How do we know? What evidence is there? When did we know? Is this the corrected number, or the number we recorded at the time?
A team accountable for a thing will grow and protect it. A team measured on its own dissolution will not.
A tribunal asks equally what the client was told.
Access for everyone
Accommodation and the signature problem
Accounts, accruals, schedules, double-entry postings, payment instructions, and money paid out now that may have to be repaid.
Added since the source
Agreements between organisations, which sit with Secure Data Exchange. The correction itself, which the context that owns the fact makes.
All twenty-one
An Excel workbook decides which queue a request joins, how urgent it is, how long it has, and where a scanned document goes. Fifty-six procedures point at it. One of its sheets maps 445 form numbers to their handling. So the priorities and service-level targets for the whole service sit outside the platform, kept up by hand.
An engine upgrade can change how the same rules evaluate.
An entitlement determined twice must not be paid twice, and that guarantee lives here rather than in five case contexts.
And together they carry what the architecture is trying to do.
Any group of clients moved to the new system can be moved back to the old one without a separate data project. An approved statement says what information would be lost on the way back. Being able to undo a move means both having a way to do it and knowing how much survives.
Appeals & Reconsideration
Apt boundaries
Archiving the software tells you what it was. It does not promise that anything in twenty years can still run it. The operating system, the processor and the container runtime all die younger than a child protection record, which the ministry keeps for ninety years.
As the first copy is made
Ask a typical case management system why a person got a particular amount in March 2022 and it will work the sum again. It uses today's rules, today's data and today's software, then reports the answer with confidence. The answer may well be right. Nobody can tell, and nobody can show a tribunal the difference.

Before the first real event, has someone chosen how each kind of fact will be destroyed, and published what survives?
Before the first rule is written
Before the system stores anything, decide how each kind of fact will be destroyed when its time comes. The default is to delete a whole kind of record on a set schedule. For some kinds of fact another method is chosen instead: keep personal details in a separate place that can be deleted, or, for a few kinds named one by one, lock one person’s records with a key and then destroy the key. Publish what is left after a record is destroyed. Plan who holds the keys. And say what a replay does when it reaches a record it can no longer read.

Does not own
Does the design name the point each decision read up to (the watermark), write it into the decision record, and set a limit on how far behind a store can be? If a store is past that limit, does the decision stop instead of going ahead?

Each benefit records whether and how a decision can be challenged
Each category has its own page. Every requirement opens to show its description, the checks that prove it is met, and the reasons it exists.
Each decision stores which version of the rules was used and which version of the facts. It stores full copies of them, not links to them. It also records what the client asked for, which requirements they met and which they didn’t, what the ministry assumed, what evidence was missing, and the date the client was told. When a tribunal rescinds a decision, the original record stays exactly as it was, marked with the rescission, and the ministry makes a new decision alongside it.
Each entry below demonstrates the first two claims. The third rests on an argument against a list of intents, and it is the weakest of the three, because another architect could reasonably draw some of these lines elsewhere.
Each kind of evidence, such as income or household composition, is registered before anyone can use it. The registration sets its shape, what counts as verifying it, how sensitive it is, how long it is kept and how it ends, and whose record it is. None of that is guessed later from where the data happens to sit.
Each object belongs to one part of the system. They are not a shared model that every part must use; each part keeps its own view of what it needs.
Each one carries a header naming its purpose, the policy it carries out, the law behind it, and how the system classifies the work. That turns the whole set into a map of the services.
Each one lists the policy obligations it meets and the design parameters that test it, and links to them.
Each parameter says how you would find out it has been broken. Where software could do that check automatically, it has to be built as an automated check.

Each part keeps its own picture of the data
Each part of the system keeps its own description of a person, a case or a payment. There is no single shared “Person” record that every part must use. No part shares a database layout with another, reads another part’s tables, or relies on a data type that another part defines.

Every parameter is necessary: take one away and the design loses something nothing else supplies.
Every principle in the architecture is accounted for. Seven carried across, with their wording narrowed or widened. Three split, because each held two ideas that could stand apart. One took in a clause from another, and one became more general. So twelve principles turned into fourteen parameters, and seven more joined them.
Every record has one system in charge of it: its system of record. That holds for each group of clients, and it still holds while clients move from the old system to the new one. The two systems never both make changes and sort out the differences afterwards. And where the data affects what a person receives, no automatic process decides which version wins. Some things that look like one record are two, each with its own writer: Financial Components writes the payment instruction, and Payments writes the payment actually sent. If the ministry has to switch to its own copy because a supplier cuts off a cloud service, it hands over which system writes, and adds the records made during the switch back in order afterwards. It never merges them.
Every recurring task a caseworker does has a written procedure: what starts it, which screens to open, which form to send, what to type in which field. Together they run to 8.2 million characters. They describe the service as staff really deliver it.
Every requirement carries acceptance criteria written as "given, when, then", so a tester can say whether it passes.
Every rule carries a label saying what kind of decision it produces. Some produce an administrative decision, which needs reasons. Some produce a decision a person has to make before it takes effect. The rest are working sums that affect nobody on their own.
Every rule comes with a way to catch it being broken
Every service has a target for how much of the time it must be working, and limits on how long it can be down and how much recent data it can lose. These targets depend on how much harm an outage does to a client. A practice run has to show the targets can be met. Anything shared by several services must meet the strictest target of any of them. The requirement for an on-premise copy of any core cloud service, monthly payments first, is one place this is already tested.

Five things stored with every decision
For any kind of fact, can you name its custodian? Does the system read that, or do people just follow a habit? And can every decision about access be traced to the register of agreements, and to nothing else?
For common tools, buy one, adopt one or reuse one. That covers workflow, notifications, sign-in, storing passwords and keys, policy checks, scheduling, document storage, search, and print and mail. To build one instead, name a legal, policy or programme need that no ready-made product meets. Someone other than the team that would own it has to agree. Wanting it sooner is not a reason.
For each entitlement, the system records four things: the law it is based on, whether a decision can be reconsidered, whether it can be appealed, and who hears the appeal. It records these for each entitlement and each variant of it. It never assumes they are the same as for the wider programme the entitlement belongs to. The list has one keeper, the decisions model, which publishes it for every other part to read.
For each parameter, name the check and say whether it runs automatically. Where a person checks something a computer could, say which one, and why nobody has automated it.
For each service, can a person finish it through every supported channel? Does the result change depending on the route? For each screen, has a person tested it with assistive technology, and not just run an automated scan? A scan catches only about 30% of problems.
For every entitlement and every variant, can the system state the law it is based on, whether it can be reconsidered, whether it can be appealed, and who hears the appeal? Can it do that without borrowing any of it from the wider programme?
For every entitlement, name who decides and who reviews, and say which powers the ministry keeps for itself. Can every decision be traced to the person who actually reasoned it through, rather than someone who only gave advice?
For every record being moved, name the one system of record and the group of clients it covers. If the answer is “it depends on the field”, someone has divided the work by field instead of by group of clients.
For every tool built in-house, name the legal, policy or programme need that no ready-made product meets. Then name who agreed to it, other than the people who built it.

The current system keeps only today's answer. It rewrites history instead of recording it. What did we know, when did we know it, and how do we prove it? This design keeps all three.

Functional requirements — The Future of Case Management IT
Gathering the facts means reading across several stores that update on their own schedules. Two decisions issued seconds apart, with one store briefly behind, can each see a different world quite legitimately. Both replay perfectly. Both are reproducible. They disagree, and nothing described so far catches it. So the design pins each snapshot to a point in the sequence of recorded events. A later reader can then tell which view of the world a decision was made against.

Identity, evidence and decisions
If a rule is spread across several places, nobody can understand it, test it or change it safely. Soon nobody can say which version of the rule is the real one. Keeping a rule with its data also means everything that writes to the data is checked the same way. A data load or a link from another system can’t slip past a rule the data enforces itself.
If it gains a column outside this definition, the shared model has been rebuilt. Treat that as a defect, not as debt.
If nobody proves a move can be undone, you find out it can’t only when you need to
If software settles a conflict on its own, a merge rule ends up making a choice that belongs to policy or to a person. And letting both systems make changes is how a short overlap quietly becomes permanent.
If the ministry decides after the legal deadline, the client’s eligibility counts from the date the decision was due, not the date it was made. So a missed deadline changes what the client is owed. A time limit the system doesn’t track leads to wrong payments, not just slow service.

Merge and split go in on day one rather than later. The audit of the previous system found duplicate records at scale, and called its search ineffective and exact-match only. No addresses, no payment details, no employment records, no relationships. Those are evidence, owned elsewhere.
No other rule catches a system that works correctly and reliably but that the people it serves can’t reach. Counts of how many people used a service hide this completely. The cost falls on clients and on front-line staff.
No other rule catches information the ministry holds lawfully being put to a use it is barred from. Policy limits five different kinds of things: a single detail in a record, a type of content, who the information goes to, a subject, and a way of communicating. Only the first has anything to do with a calculation.
No other rule makes sure recovery is planned. Every recovery figure in the architecture covers the reporting and analytics platform. None covers the published interface, the translation layer, the decision service or the case records. And getting the system running again doesn’t fix a payment run that was missed.
No other rule says who is allowed to use which power. The decision record shows what was decided and by whom. But it does nothing to stop one person deciding, reviewing and releasing the money. Policy sets out all three of these separations directly.
No part reads another part's database
No requirement matches these filters.
No shared tables. No joins across schemas. Not for a report, and not in a test environment. This rule erodes first, and takes the longest to notice.

One master in place of the five places such an entitlement is held today. Refusing one can be challenged, so it is a decision, not a setting.
One parameter is not about the system at all. N18 ranges over the other twenty. It makes each of them name how you catch a breach, and it says that anything you could write as a lint rule or a compatibility check has to be written as one.
One per program family
One registered kind matters more than it looks: a worker’s judgement. Much of the work is a worker using a discretion the law gives them. The system records that as evidence too, as a discretionary determination. It names the law that gives the discretion, the authority the worker acted under, who decided, the evidence they weighed, and their reasons in their own words. A decision that rests on judgement can then be re-run like one that rests on arithmetic. Without it, the judgement ends up in case notes, and the decision rests on something nobody can find.

Provider & Outcome Management
Published events and the boundary test
Published interfaces use the words of policy and of the ministry’s work, not the terms of whatever product sits behind them. The interface is meant to last. The translation layer that connects it to the old system is temporary, and the team that runs it is set up to wind down.
Pure: no clock, no database, no service calls.
Pure: no input or output, no clock reads, no database access, no service calls. No rules engine gives you this on its own. The shell around the engine enforces it. The engine runs in-process against a snapshot passed by value, and that is what puts byte-identical replay within reach rather than in the brochure.

Quality requirements — The Future of Case Management IT
Rate tables, program codes, value lists and reason codes are each kept in one place and published as events. Nobody maintains a second copy by hand. They change when policy changes, not when the software does.
Rather than leave that hanging, the design commits to a horizon in three stages and writes it down in advance.
Re-running a decision proves what the rules worked out. It does not prove the rules matched the policy in force at the time. So every rule carries the policy it comes from and the date that policy took effect. The ministry does not publish old versions of its policy manual, and its archive of old rate tables has gaps. So for each family of rules the horizon also records how far back the policy itself can still be produced. Before that date, the stored reasoning, the letter and the facts are the record, and the ministry says so in advance.

Skip to content
So the unit the system records, and the unit its parts exchange, is an assertion:
Some pieces are shared infrastructure rather than parts of the business. Platform teams own them and everyone uses them. The difference matters. A platform part that starts holding program state has quietly become a twentieth domain model, and nobody chartered it.
Some requirements depend on decisions nobody has made yet: rulings on conflicts inside policy, the records schedules, and several architecture decisions. The
Some requirements pull against each other. These conflicts come from the sources themselves: policy against practice, one design parameter against another, a legal duty against a design property. Each one says what was chosen, what it costs, and who decides.
Someone can challenge a decision about their entitlement years after the ministry made it. So the design treats every decision as something you re-run, not something you remember.
Sometimes the ministry is allowed to hold a piece of information but not to use it for a certain purpose. That limit is attached to the information itself, and it goes with every copy. The system enforces the limit at the moment someone tries to use the information. It doesn’t rely on staff remembering a procedure.
Sometimes the ministry writes to a client before it decides: this is what we found, this is what it may mean, reply by this date. That letter is not a decision, and the system keeps it separate from one. It carries its reasons, its reply-by date and a plain statement that no decision has been made. Whatever the client sends back is recorded as evidence for the decision that follows.

The smallest rule surface, which is why it is captured first.
The stored reasoning, the letter and the facts are the record. Re-running stops being on offer. This is what a paper file has always been.
The system holds every legal time limit in one place: the appeals and reconsideration model releases them, and every other part uses them rather than building its own. Each limit records what starts the clock, how long it runs, what extensions are allowed, and who must approve each one. Missing a deadline is recorded as an event. Where policy says missing it has a consequence, the system applies it without anyone having to ask.
The system keeps a permanent history that is never changed. The law sometimes requires records to be destroyed. Those two pull against each other. Settle it after the first record is stored and you are rebuilding, not repairing. Timing is the whole point: a correct plan that arrives late has still failed.
The system knows whose record it is
The system never stores a fact on its own. With every fact it keeps four things: who reported it, the period of time it was true for, the date this system learned it, and the date the old system recorded it. If the old system’s date can’t be read, the record says so.

This is what makes it possible to re-run a decision and get exactly the same answer, in practice and not just in theory. A rules service that fetches its own information ties every decision to systems that must still be running. That is the first thing a tribunal will look at.
This is what makes it possible to replace the old system one piece at a time. The interface published today in front of the old system is the same one published later in front of the new services. Mix up the interface with the translation layer and you tie the old system’s words to the new design. That is the very problem the programme exists to fix.

A replacement must not do the same.

Those last four are the interesting ones, because nobody found them by thinking harder about the architecture. They came from reading what the ministry already tells its own staff to do. Policy sets time limits, and missing one changes what a client is owed. It names which entitlements a client can appeal, and to whom. It keeps the person who decides apart from the person who reviews. And it bars certain uses of information the ministry may lawfully hold. The twelve could not express any of that.

Three systems
Three things have shifted underneath since March 2022. Policy changed. The person's recorded circumstances changed, perhaps several times. And someone upgraded the software. A rules engine upgrade can change how the same rule reads, and nobody notices until a client appeals.
Time spent building tools that already exist is time not spent on getting decisions right, and that is what the programme will be judged on. Without someone else checking, the team marks its own homework. That is how this goes wrong today.
To gather the facts for a decision, the system reads from several stores. Each store updates on its own schedule, so some may be a little behind. The decision records the exact point it read up to. There is a limit on how far behind a store may be, and if one is further behind than that, the system won’t issue the decision.
To see how one business rule works, how many systems do you have to open? If it’s more than one, say which is the real source, why the others exist, and how they are produced from it.

Twelve families were drawn when the architecture was first issued, which made sixteen models. Two decisions made moments apart can disagree
Two ministries run case management: Children and Family Development, and Social Development and Poverty Reduction. The work covers assistance payments, service requests, social work, loss recovery and client support. All of it depends on a worker seeing the full picture. The work is life-critical. A wrong answer means someone might not eat this month, or a child misses a check-in.
Two ministries with broad mandates carry a very mixed portfolio. The current system forces all of it into one rigid model. That is how a design turns brittle. Here each program family gets its own model.
Two of them are worth naming, because their charters point in opposite directions on purpose. The published interface is permanent: it is the contract built to outlive whatever implements it. The translation layer over the existing Siebel system is temporary, and the team that builds it answers for winding itself up.
Two systems
Two systems do the work. One is an Oracle Siebel customer relationship management product, adapted for government. The other is a mainframe built in 1982. They run side by side and share the core programs between them. Every attempt to retire the mainframe has stalled or failed.
Two time axes are standard. This design carries a third, because the new system inherits fifteen years of records from systems that are still running.

What every part must do
What happens next is well documented. A child protection investigation and a child care subsidy renewal have almost nothing in common beyond involving a person. Make them share a lifecycle and every change to one has to be negotiated with everyone else. Multiply that over dozens of programs and nobody can change the model at all. So teams bolt on sub-entities, extend them, and add more ways to integrate. The system turns into a plate of spaghetti. You cannot change anything in one place, and any failure reaches everywhere. This is not hypothetical. ICM merged its final two phases and cut child protection scope for exactly this reason.
What happens to decisions already made from the old copy is a policy choice. Each program family sets it, and keeps it as a versioned rule. There are three answers. Re-open: make a fresh decision on the corrected facts. Annotate only: the outcome does not change, so the decision record notes the correction and why nothing followed. Flag for review: nobody can tell mechanically whether it matters, often because a worker’s judgement was one of the inputs, so a person decides.

When a decision is challenged
When a fact is corrected, every copy has to act
When a part copies evidence, it records where the copy came from: which part, which piece of evidence, which version, when the source learned it, and when the copy was taken. That is what makes rule four checkable. A correction can find every copy by looking it up, not by asking every team.
When every part shares one model, any change to it has to wait for everyone who uses it. One team’s release holds up all the others. ICM ran into exactly this: it had to merge its last two phases and drop child protection from its scope.
When one part copies a fact from another, it records where the copy came from. If the source later corrects the fact, you can list everyone who holds a copy, and each of them has to deal with the change. That is true even when a decision has already gone out based on the old value. What each program does about such a decision is set by policy for that program: decide again, note the correction on the record, or send it to a person to judge.
When one part of the system sends something to another, it sends a fact with its source, or a decision. It doesn’t send rows copied out of its database, ID numbers only it understands, or the raw results of a search.
When someone is paid too much, the money falls into one of two classes. If the client's circumstances changed and they told the ministry late, it is a recoverable overpayment. The ministry takes it back at $10 a month, out of a payment that was already only just enough. If the ministry held the information all along and did not act on it, that is administrative error, and the client should not carry it.

Who does what, and by when.
Who is responsible for a record, its custodian, is something the system stores and reads, not something people just know. The system properly handles records that belong to someone other than the provincial government, such as an Indigenous Nation, instead of forcing them into the wrong shape.
